passages.text: Computer-based technologies called immersive design tools are changing how construction projects are planned and built. These technologies allow builders to test ideas, solve problems, and improve designs in the virtual world, before using any real materials or spending lots of time. For example, architects could explore digital blueprints to spot issues early, and builders wearing special glasses could see virtual instructions as they look at a building, reducing mistakes. Cities could use these tools to plan major projects, like subway systems. Immersive design tools can also train construction workers in realistic digital environments, teaching them new skills safely. While virtual tools could make building more efficient, challenges like high costs, privacy concerns, and potential changes to construction jobs still need to be addressed. With continued creativity, virtual tools could make construction faster, safer, and better for the planet, transforming how we shape the spaces where we live, work, and play.

Digital twins take this even further by creating a virtual copy of a real object, system, or space. Digital twins are used in many fields—everything from medicine, where digital twins of the human body can help doctors, to construction, where they can track the progress of a project (to read about a digital twin of the Earth used to predict flooding, see this article). These digital models can be updated with live data, helping people understand, improve, and manage complex systems. A digital twin of a bridge, for example, could be updated with live data from sensors on the actual bridge, tracking construction progress and identifying potential weak points, helping engineers to fix problems before they happen. By allowing builders to test ideas and solve problems virtually, digital twins save time, materials, and money.

The construction industry is also dealing with a labor shortage, which means there are not enough skilled workers to meet the growing demand for new buildings and infrastructure. In the United States alone, hundreds of thousands of additional workers will be needed in the coming years to keep up with demand [4]. This shortage increases costs and makes it harder to complete projects on time. Immersive technologies could help by transforming how workers are trained. VR simulations let trainees practice skills in a realistic digital environment, no matter where they are. For example, a new builder could learn how to install wiring or operate heavy machinery before even stepping into a real construction site. This speeds up training, makes the work safer, and ensures workers are better prepared for the challenges of their jobs.

passages.text: However, soil inorganic carbon (SIC), which comprises primarily carbonate minerals, has historically been treated as a relatively stable, geogenic pool with limited biogeochemical relevance on management timescales [10]. This perception began to shift only in recent years, as accumulating evidence showed that SIC is in fact dynamic and responsive to environmental forcing [11,12]. For instance, a global meta-analysis of land use change effects on SIC revealed that conversions from grassland to farmland can increase SIC by up to 30.6%, whereas grassland restoration may reduce it by 14.4%, demonstrating that SIC responses are directionally opposite to those of SOC in many contexts [10]. Parallel to land use effects, climate-change factors have also been shown to influence SIC dynamics: regional drought events and elevated atmospheric CO2 concentrations can promote inorganic carbon accumulation via accelerated carbonate precipitation and the CO2 fertilization effect, respectively [13–15].

Collectively, these findings suggest that SOC and SIC do not respond independently. Rather, they exist in a state of dynamic equilibrium that regulates the net direction of soil carbon sources and sinks [16]. Despite the well-documented individual responses of SOC and SIC to land use and climate change, the soil carbon source/sink effects arising from the dynamic equilibrium of these two components have been consistently overlooked and underquantified. For instance, large-scale vegetation restoration projects have been implemented in Northern China to enhance carbon sequestration, but if grazing intensity is not properly regulated, soil carbon loss driven by grassland degradation could offset the sequestration benefits achieved through restoration in some areas [16]. Therefore, to thoroughly investigate how soil carbon sources and sinks respond to abrupt land use change within the broader context of environmental change, it is essential to systematically elucidate the dynamics of the SCP by quantifying the coupled responses of organic and inorganic carbon pools during land use conversions.

To bridge this gap, structural equation modeling (SEM) has gradually been brought into ecological and soil science research. SEM was originally developed and widely applied in the social sciences [5,23], but it has since been adapted to test causal pathways in vegetation-soil-climate systems. However, conventional SEM relies on maximum likelihood estimation and imposes stringent demands on sample size, requirements that are frequently unmet in regional-scale soil surveys [24]. In this study, partial least squares SEM (PLS-SEM) offers a more practical alternative, especially when sample sizes are limited and multiple latent variables are present [25]. It is important to recognize that PLS-SEM has inferential limitations compared with ML-SEM, such as potential biases in path estimations, the lack of global goodness-of-fit indices, and sensitivity to indicator selection [26,27]. Even so, when the research objective emphasizes prediction and theory development rather than strict theory confirmation, PLS-SEM proves useful for dissecting SCP dynamics driven by multifactorial interactions [27].

This study aims to investigate the response of SCP dynamics to intense land use type change under the influence of global and environmental change. It seeks to clarify the role of land use change in soil carbon processes and quantify the contributions of environmental and land use change to SCP dynamics. Specifically, based on soil sample data from the 1980s and 2010s, this research employs a random forest (RF) feature selection framework to spatially predict SOC and SIC. Building upon this foundation, the study integrates SOC and SIC to estimate regional SCP in Northern China. Subsequently, a PLS-SEM is employed to couple soil carbon dynamics with climate changes (encompassing biotic, climatic, and nitrogen deposition) under different land use changes. This approach aims to reveal the dynamic evolution of SCP and its sources/sinks under the dual drivers of intense human activities and complex environmental changes, thereby achieving the research objectives. Based on the above research background and purpose, this study proposes the following core assumptions:

It is important to emphasize that the R² values for single land use type contrast sharply with the substantially higher values observed for conversion pathways, particularly those involving unused land. This divergence reflects a scale-dependency in driver dominance within a single land use type, soil carbon is strongly modulated by fine-scale management factors (irrigation, fertilization, grazing intensity, tillage) that are highly heterogeneous and largely unobserved at the regional extent, leaving substantial residual variance [50]. Previous studies at the county scale have demonstrated that population density and local agricultural management can explain over 30% of SOC variance, often exceeding the explanatory power of climate and topography [51]. However, such management variables are not available as spatially continuous, long-term datasets for Northern China, and their omission accounts for the unexplained variance in CUL and GRA models. By contrast, land use conversion constitutes a strong directional perturbation that reorganizes carbon pools along macro-scale biophysical gradients, making the response more predictable from the climate, terrain, and soil variables captured in our models. Thus, the lower R² for CUL and GRA does not indicate model deficiency, but rather the inherent limitation of explaining management-driven micro-heterogeneity with coarse-resolution regional predictors [52].

The interpretation of our findings requires careful consideration of the 30-year temporal scale of arid-region soil carbon dynamics. The national soil survey data employed in this study provide bulk SOC stocks without physical or chemical fractionation into labile, slow, or mineral-associated pools. In the semi-arid and arid soils, this bulk measurement is dominated by relatively stable, mineral-associated organic carbon, which is inherently buffered against rapid change by strong organo-mineral interactions and long-term pedogenic controls. From this perspective, the statistically significant changes in SOC stock distribution and vertical allocation observed across the two survey periods are particularly noteworthy. They indicated that land use change has already perturbed the soil carbon system sufficiently to overcome the high background spatial variance imposed by parent material heterogeneity. Furthermore, the concurrent changes in SIC stocks, which respond more sensitively to decadal-scale perturbations in hydrological regimes, irrigation, and CO2 dynamics, provide complementary evidence that land use change has initiated measurable carbon cycle reorganization within this timeframe. We therefore interpret our results as capturing a transient, management-sensitive phase of soil carbon reconfiguration rather than a pedogenic equilibrium. These early-stage trajectories are critical for land management decision-making, as they reveal the directional sensitivity of SCPs to land use change before long-term stabilization processes fully manifest.

Northern China was a stable net soil carbon source during the study period, with the same decreases in both SOC and SIC, indicating that soil carbon losses did not occur only due to changes in a single carbon pool but instead from the combined effects of coordinated responses across SCP. Consequently, Northern China remains a net contributor to terrestrial carbon emissions under current global climate and land use changes, imposing direct constraints on regional carbon neutrality pathway assessments. This coordinated depletion of both organic and inorganic pools carries critical implications for regional carbon management: it suggests that carbon mitigation strategies focusing exclusively on SOC enhancement (e.g., through soil amendments or land retirement) may be insufficient, as concurrent SIC losses could offset overall soil carbon gains. Therefore, effective carbon neutrality pathways in Northern China must adopt a dual-pool accounting framework rather than relying on single-pool assessments. This result is consistent with our assumption (1).

Existing research predominantly highlights increasing trends in SOC within surface soils of northern hemisphere farmlands [53,54], and the findings of increased SOC in cropland from this study are consistent with those existing results. Some studies have also demonstrated profile differentiation in SOC dynamics. For instance, SOC increased in the 0–20 cm layer of paddy soils on the Chengdu Plain but decreased in deeper layers from the 1980s to the 2010s [55], and also increased in the 0–40 cm layer on the Guanzhong Plain but decreased in the 40–100 cm layer [29]. These study areas contained extensive intensively CUL under active human regulation and focus on SOC variations at different soil depths, but they are inapplicable to large-scale regions dominated by natural and semi-natural systems. Northern China is characterized by GRA and UNU as the primary land use types, and distinct patterns were found when analyzed at the 1-m soil profile scale. GRA was a strong net carbon source, whereas UNU represented a substantial carbon sinks, highlighting the dominant regulatory role of land use types in shaping soil carbon sources/sinks patterns. This conclusion shows the need to clearly distinguish between different land use types and their corresponding soil carbon responses and mechanisms when assessing terrestrial ecosystem carbon sources and sinks.

Previous studies have established that land use change significantly alters soil carbon dynamics, but most have focused on single carbon pools or specific conversion types without disentangling the divergent responses of SOC and SIC to environmental drivers [10,56–58]. This study reveals that irrespective of the specific conversion pathway, transitions from CUL consistently result in SOC accumulation alongside SIC reduction. Specifically, during these CUL outflow processes, the positive response of SOC to climate change is substantially enhanced, primarily driven by increased precipitation and a shift towards wetter climatic conditions. This finding is consistent with prior work demonstrating that moisture enrichment benefits SOC sequestration but inhibits SIC stabilization [59]. However, we extend these earlier findings by showing that long-term intense tillage disturbances characteristic of historical CUL management, coupled with soil acidification induced by atmospheric nitrogen deposition, likely exacerbate carbonate dissolution and leaching [35,60]. Thus, by integrating land use history with biogeochemical processes, our results provide a mechanistic explanation for the observed phenomenon that SOC accumulation in CUL systems is systematically accompanied by SIC loss.

Regarding FOR–GRA conversion, existing research suggests that highly productive natural vegetation types favor synergistic carbon sequestration across multiple pools [61,62]. Our findings corroborate and extend this view that such conversion enhances accumulation in both carbon pools, primarily driven by sustained carbon inputs from increased leaf area index and gross primary productivity alongside relatively stable soil chemistry. In contrast to prior studies that have emphasized biotic controls on SOC, our results further reveal that after FOR transitions to CUL or UNU, SOC remains primarily positively driven by biotic factors, whereas SIC exhibits heightened sensitivity to climate and shows a declining trend. This distinction underscores a critical insight from our work, namely that human disturbance poses distinct risks to SIC stability that have been insufficiently addressed in previous research.

Extensive GRA degradation in Northern China has been caused by overgrazing [63], with declining vegetation productivity and soil erosion leading to substantial soil carbon loss. Our results demonstrate that soil carbon sources in northern GRA were characterized by the combined loss of SOC and SIC, where the loss of SIC was dominant. Path analysis based on PLS-SEM indicated that climate change was a key driver of inorganic carbon loss from GRA soils, and this climatic signal was primarily dominated by reduced precipitation and a decreased PDSI. Decreased precipitation directly weakens GRA water regulation and carbon sequestration functions [64]. Even under high-emission scenarios, the enhanced water use efficiency resulting from elevated atmospheric CO2 concentrations can hardly offset the severe negative impacts of drought on SCP, demonstrating that the inherent vulnerability of GRA, combined with external climatic stresses, collectively leads to the loss of SCP dominated by SIC.

The results show that UNU as a vast potential carbon sink in Northern China, but it also reveals a concurrent increase in both SOC and SIC after UNU–CUL conversion. This result is a pattern that contradicts not only our speculation (2) but also the prevailing view in the literature that cropland expansion depletes SIC stocks through tillage-induced disturbance and enhanced leaching [65,66]. The PLS-SEM analysis offers a mechanistic basis for this divergence. For SIC, the path from UNU–CUL to biological variables indicated that the establishment of CUL vegetation stimulated biological activity, which in turn promoted SIC accumulation. This aligns with the biological carbonate pump operating in arid ecosystems that enhanced root and microbial respiration elevates soil CO2 concentrations, facilitating carbonate dissolution in the rhizosphere, subsequent capillary rise and evaporative concentration then precipitate secondary carbonates in surface horizons [67,68]. N-deposition were strongly positively linked to SIC suggests that irrigation with Ca² ⁺ /HCO3−-rich water and nitrogen fertilization in newly converted CUL likely shifted soil chemical equilibria toward carbonate precipitation, overriding the SIC-depleting effects of tillage documented in other agroecosystems [69]. Notably, this mechanism applies specifically to the converted CUL, whereas the SIC accrual observed in UNU itself cannot draw on irrigation or fertilization and must therefore be sustained by aeolian Ca supply. At the observed accrual rate of 2.68 g C m-2 yr-2 (8.03 t ha-1 over 30 years), the stoichiometric Ca demand for ~22 g CaCO3 m-2 yr-1 is consistent with measured dust-borne carbonate deposition in this region (11–54 g CaCO3 m-2 yr-1) [70,71]. For SOC, the observed increase was primarily driven by anthropogenic carbon inputs [72,73]. In contrast to studies that identify SIC as a sensitive early indicator of land use change, our findings suggest that in severely degraded arid lands, anthropogenic inputs (irrigation and fertilization) and biological carbonate pumping can transiently mask the SIC-depletion signal, rendering SIC a poor early-warning indicator in such contexts.

In general, our findings reveal that soil carbon responses to global change were shaped by land use type and require explicit consideration of both organic and inorganic pools. By demonstrating divergent SOC and SIC dynamics across natural, semi-natural, and managed systems, this study challenges the conventional focus on surface SOC in farmlands and underscores the critical role of SIC in regional carbon budgets, particularly in arid and semi-arid zones. Practically, the stark contrasts between carbon sources and sinks highlight that carbon neutrality strategies must be land use-specific and should safeguard GRA from degradation and drought, harness UNU sequestration potential, and acknowledge SIC losses accompanying agricultural transitions. Incorporating such dual-pool, land use-differentiated frameworks into carbon accounting and climate mitigation planning is therefore essential for realistic regional carbon neutrality assessments.

Results of this study demonstrate that land use change can reshape soil carbon dynamics as our speculation (3), primarily manifested in two main ways. First, altering land use types can reverse regional carbon losses due to the strong coupling between soil carbon sources-sinks and regional land use type changes. This transformation can shift the carbon source patterns for GRA, endowing them with significant carbon sink potential. After land use conversion from GRA (to CUL, FOR, or UNU), soil carbon sinks may form through synergistic changes in the SOC and SIC pools. In particular, this transformation frequently reverses the response of SIC to precipitation from positive to negative, thereby exacerbating its sensitivity. This reversal likely reflects a shift in the dominant hydrological control on carbonate dynamics. Moderate precipitation may favor carbonate precipitation via reduced leaching and evaporative concentration under GRA. However, altered soil hydrology and root water uptake may lower soil water potentials below thresholds required for Ca²⁺ and HCO3− transport after GRA conversion, particularly to CUL or FOR, disrupting precipitation kinetics and rendering SIC more vulnerable to drought-induced depletion [10,74,75].

Second, our results demonstrate that land use change not only reversed soil carbon sources and sinks but also played a crucial role in amplifying soil carbon dynamics per unit area. After land use conversion, the magnitude of the total soil carbon change increased significantly. In addition, both SOC and SIC exhibited stronger responses to environmental variables, including land use, biological factors, climate, and nitrogen deposition. Thus, land use change altered the direction of soil carbon sources/sinks but also heightened the variability and uncertainty of SCP. Land use conversion markedly increased the sensitivity of soil carbon dynamics to climate change, where SOC primarily responded to climate shifts whereas SIC was more strongly driven by the CO2 concentration. The response of SOC to climate change markedly intensified after land use conversion, reflecting the high sensitivity of the vegetation cover, litter input, and microbial processes to temperature and moisture variations [67,68,72]. By contrast, SIC exhibited a significantly heightened response to changes in the atmospheric CO2 concentration, with a particularly marked increase in the sensitivity of its leaching-precipitation balance in response to variations in atmospheric CO2 partial pressure. Land use changes further strengthened the coupling between SIC and atmospheric carbon by influencing the soil carbonate leaching-precipitation balance and soil hydrological processes. This functional division of labor between SOC and SIC in terms of their primary controlling factors was difficult to discern in previous studies that often analyzed them together.

This study reveals that Northern China functioned as a net soil carbon source from the 1980s to the 2010s, driven by coordinated SOC and SIC losses. Land use type was strongly associated with carbon source/sink patterns, with GRA acting as a source via SIC depletion and UNU as a sink through SIC accumulation. Notably, SOC responded primarily to biotic drivers, whereas SIC showed heightened sensitivity to climate and CO2 fluctuations, revealing a functional division between pools. These findings challenge the prevailing single-pool paradigm and underscore the necessity of dual-pool accounting in terrestrial carbon assessments. From a management perspective, differentiated strategies are needed: controlling grazing to mitigate SIC loss in GRA and prioritizing ecological restoration to harness SIC sequestration in UNU. Regional carbon neutrality frameworks must explicitly incorporate SIC to avoid underestimating land use effects. We acknowledge greater uncertainty in deeper layer predictions below 80 cm and limited inter-annual resolution. Future work should employ stratified covariates and process-based models to improve accuracy and validate these pathways at broader scales.

passages.text: The High Mountain Asia (HMA) region contains the largest concentration of glaciers outside the polar regions and provides critical water resources for several major Asian river systems, including the Yangtze and Yellow Rivers in China and numerous transboundary rivers in South and Southeast Asia. However, HMA is experiencing rapid cryospheric change under accelerated warming, with surface temperatures increasing at a rate of 0.3 ± 0.2 °C per decade, exceeding the global mean warming rate of 0.2 ± 0.1 °C per decade [3]. This pronounced warming has resulted in widespread glacier retreat and enhanced mass loss across the region, with profound implications for global sea-level rise, regional water availability, ecosystem stability, and cryosphere-related hazards [4]. Therefore, accurately quantifying glacier mass balance in HMA is essential for understanding glacier–climate interactions and assessing future water-resource and hazard risks.

Despite extensive investigations, the persistence and evolution of the Karakoram Anomaly remain unresolved. Some studies suggest that the anomaly has persisted into the 2010s and even the 2020s, with glaciers maintaining near-equilibrium mass balance in recent decades [6], whereas others indicate that the anomaly has weakened or transitioned toward net mass loss, particularly after 2015 [2]. Moreover, the timing and spatial pattern of anomaly evolution remain debated, with some studies suggesting an earlier decline around 2010–2015, while others report continued positive mass balance in parts of the western Karakoram into the 2020s, implying possible regional differences in the decay of the anomaly [7]. The recent anomalous trends in the Karakoram and the heterogeneity of glacier mass balance across its various sub-regions remain unclear. Addressing these questions is particularly important because the Karakoram hosts numerous surge-type glaciers and rapidly evolving glacier lakes, which can alter downstream runoff regimes and increase the potential risk of glacier-related hazards such as glacier lake outburst floods (GLOFs). Therefore, an updated, high-resolution assessment of glacier mass balance across the entire Karakoram is urgently needed.

Despite these advances, existing studies have mainly focused on long-term regional averages or estimates derived from individual observation systems. Consequently, the coupled evolution of glacier mass balance, spatio-temporal heterogeneity remains insufficiently understood. In this study, we integrate ICESat-2 observations with DEMs derived from ASTER stereo imagery and the SRTM DEM within a unified reference framework to investigate glacier mass changes across the Karakoram from 2000 to 2024. Specifically, this study aims to (1) investigate phased and high-resolution analysis of glacier mass balance spanning 2000–2024 and characterize the temporal evolution of the Karakoram anomaly; (2) quantify the spatial heterogeneity of glacier mass changes across 17 basins; and (3) assess the relative contributions of topographic and climatic factors to the observed spatial variability in glacier mass balance Overall, this study reveals a more detailed spatio-temporal evolution of glacier mass balance in the Karakoram region, providing an important reference for understanding the Karakoram Anomaly and regional water resource management.

To examine spatial variations in greater detail, the Karakoram region was subdivided into 17 sub-basins based on the HydroATLAS database. Glacier mass balance varied substantially among the 17 sub-basins, with relatively positive or near-equilibrium conditions in the northern and central Karakoram but stronger mass loss in several southern and eastern basins. Specifically, basins 13, 14, and 12 in the northern and central Karakoram exhibited slight glacier accumulation, whereas basins 4, 6, 8, and 11 in the southern and eastern Karakoram experienced mass loss. Among all sub-basins, Basin 8 underwent the most pronounced glacier loss, with a mass balance of −0.35 ± 0.027 m w.e. a − ¹, while basin 7 showed the highest glacier gain, at 0.067 ± 0.006 m w.e. a − ¹.

In this study, glacier mass balance over the past 25 years was quantified across multiple spatial and temporal scales by combining ASTER DEM and ICESat-2 datasets. The results indicate that prior to 2010, glaciers across the Karakoram generally experienced accumulation, consistent with the previously reported Karakoram anomaly [37]. Post-2010, although the overall glacier state transitioned toward mass loss, the anomaly did not entirely vanish; instead, it exhibited distinct regional and temporal characteristics. Spatially, positive mass balance persisted primarily in the northern Karakoram (e.g., basins 12 and 14) and central regions (basins 1 and 7). Temporally, analysis of interannual and seasonal variations suggests a reappearance of the anomaly between 2018 and 2020. In contrast, the southeastern Karakoram (e.g., basins 6, 8, and 11) experienced continuous mass loss, indicating that the anomaly had largely disappeared in this area. After 2020, most basins showed net mass depletion, with only a few eastern basins retaining minor positive trends, suggesting that the regional expression of the anomaly had substantially weakened and become spatially restricted. Whether this anomaly will re-emerge in the future remains uncertain, underscoring the need for continued monitoring.

The discrepancies between our results and previous studies can largely be attributed to differences in data sources, spatio-temporal scope, topographic correction, and density parameters. First, the ASTER‑derived mass balance is more negative than the ICESat‑2 estimate for the overlapping period. This discrepancy likely stems from differences in spatial sampling: ASTER DEMs provide near‑complete coverage of the glacier surface, including high‑altitude accumulation zones that may have experienced thinning over the longer ASTER period, whereas ICESat‑2 footprints are potentially located in lower‑elevation, flatter areas that may have experienced milder changes. Additionally, the higher spatial resolution of ASTER DEMs may capture localized, intense ablation features that are missed by the sparse ICESat‑2 footprints. Consequently, the ASTER-derived mass loss rate (−0.073 ± 0.06) for 2000–2022 is markedly higher than the altimetry-derived rate.

Although ERA5-Land provides one of the highest-resolution global reanalysis datasets currently available (~9 km), its spatial resolution remains insufficient to fully resolve the pronounced topographic complexity of the Karakoram, where elevation differences commonly exceed 5,000 m within individual grid cells [49]. Consequently, local topoclimatic processes, including valley circulations, glacier-induced katabatic winds, and terrain-related radiative effects, are inevitably smoothed in the reanalysis, potentially affecting glacier-scale climate forcing. Previous evaluations in the Himalaya have similarly shown that ERA5-Land performs well at representing regional climatic variability but cannot adequately reproduce local atmospheric processes without further statistical or dynamical downscaling [49]. Therefore, the relationships between glacier mass balance and climatic variables identified in this study should be interpreted as regional-scale associations rather than glacier-specific climatic responses. Future work integrating high-resolution regional climate models and field observations will help better resolve these local processes.

passages.text: The natural forests of Picea schrenkiana var. tianschanica in the Central Tianshan Mountains of Xinjiang represent a critical ecological barrier for water conservation, biodiversity maintenance, and carbon sequestration in arid and semi-arid regions of Northwest China [17,18]. These forests develop under pronounced topographic gradients and distinct stand structures, which strongly influence soil structure development and nutrient dynamics [19,20]. Despite substantial progress in understanding soil structural dynamics, existing studies on forest soil aggregation have largely examined single drivers (e.g., topography or vegetation) in isolation, or have relied on bivariate correlations that fail to separate direct effects from indirect pathways mediated by soil properties. Consequently, for high-altitude Picea schrenkiana var. tianschanica forests, evidence remains scarce regarding how topography and stand structure jointly regulate SAS across soil depths and through which specific pathways (e.g., organic matter, moisture, bulk density) these controls operate. Furthermore, recent stand-development work highlights that forest development can systematically shift aggregate-size distribution and strengthen aggregate-associated carbon protection, emphasizing the necessity of explicitly integrating stand age and structural trajectories into stability assessments [21].

Several limitations constrain inference. First, the sample represents one experimental forest in the central Tianshan Mountains, so extrapolation to other forest types or climatic regions requires caution. Second, the design was observational; MEM adjusts for measured covariates, while RDA and SEM describe multivariate and hypothesized directional associations, but none establishes causation. Third, the SEM explained 23.1% of SAS variance, leaving substantial variation unaccounted for; global fit indices may also be uninformative if the model is just identified. Fourth, the study did not measure microbial community composition, fungal hyphae, root traits or exudates, litter quantity and chemistry, soil texture/mineralogy, or freeze–thaw and wetting–drying histories. Finally, plots were sampled during different field seasons rather than repeatedly through time, preventing direct assessment of seasonal or interannual dynamics. Long-term repeated measurements combined with microbial, root, mineralogical, and hydrological data are needed to test the proposed mechanisms.

passages.text: The controversy centered on the whereabouts and handling of paintings from the Pang family’s 1959 donation to the Nanjing Museum. Public attention intensified after the Jiangnan Chun scroll attributed to Qiu Ying, one of the donated works, appeared in a Beijing auction preview in 2025, prompting questions about how donated paintings had left or become unaccounted for in the museum’s collection. The dispute also raised questions about earlier authenticity assessments and the procedures through which several donated works had been removed from the collection and transferred into market circulation. Media reporting intensified public attention in December 2025, and the museum issued a statement on 17 December. On 23 December 2025, the National Cultural Heritage Administration announced that a working group had arrived in Nanjing [17]. On the same day, provincial authorities established an investigation group involving discipline inspection, public security, cultural heritage, and other relevant agencies [18]. Subsequent developments kept the conduct of the investigation under sustained public scrutiny. The official findings, released on 9 February 2026, attributed irregularities in the 1990s disposal process to former museum leadership and announced that twenty-four individuals would be investigated and dealt with in accordance with applicable rules and law [19]. The museum issued a public apology on the same day.

The analysis uses 64,349 publicly visible top-level comments organized into three event-anchored source-content groups. Content group A contains comments attached to source content associated with the museum’s initial statement and the regulatory intervention of 17 to 23 December 2025. Content group B contains comments attached to source content associated with the continuing investigation and related developments between 27 and 30 December 2025. Content group C contains comments attached to source content associated with the official findings, the apology, and subsequent discussion between 9 and 27 February 2026. These groups are not comment-posting time bins. Comment posting dates overlap across groups, and comments attached to content from earlier phases continue to appear after later anchor events. The comparison identifies differences among event-anchored discourse settings and does not estimate a temporal progression of public opinion.

The first analytical task concerns the substantive organization of public judgment. Topic modeling allows recurrent concerns to emerge from the corpus without reducing comments to a single sentiment measure and without imposing the three accountability functions directly on individual comments. The analysis separates model-derived topic discovery from researcher-developed higher-order coding. First-order topics were identified inductively through topic modeling. The higher-order thematic framework was developed through an earlier stage of independent coding by two coders followed by consensus discussion, and was subsequently fixed for a separate independent validation round. The three-layer framework provides an interpretive lens for considering how the resulting thematic groupings relate to affective expression, responsibility attribution, and legitimacy questioning; these layers are not treated as separately measured dimensions.

Changes in the communication environment have expanded the settings in which this vulnerability becomes visible. Public expectations increasingly emphasize transparency, responsiveness, and stakeholder inclusion [29,30]. The channels through which institutions are evaluated have also expanded. Platform discourse now operates alongside traditional media and professional evaluation as an additional setting in which institutional reputation is contested and renegotiated. Existing research on museum legitimacy has mainly examined institutional environments, governance structures, and internal processes of legitimacy maintenance and repair [7,15]. Less attention has been given to platform-mediated public judgment as a continuing source of external legitimacy pressure. Cultural institutions must therefore address both the precipitating incident and the public interpretations through which it becomes a test of custodial responsibility, procedural integrity, and institutional trust.

Accountability describes a relationship in which an actor is obliged to explain and justify conduct to a forum that can pose questions, render judgment, and impose consequences [31,32]. It operates as an ongoing process linking institutional actors to evaluative forums. Governance research distinguishes horizontal accountability among peer organizations, civil society groups, and media outlets from vertical accountability to hierarchical authorities [33]. Several accountability types may operate concurrently. Democratic accountability concerns responsiveness to public mandates. Professional accountability concerns adherence to expertise-based standards. Managerial accountability concerns the discharge of delegated responsibilities [34,35]. Cultural institutions may face all of these forms. Museums answer to professional communities on curatorial integrity, to funders and governing bodies on stewardship, and to broader publics on mission and trust [15,16].

The connection between platformization and museum legitimacy explains why platform-mediated discourse creates distinctive pressures for cultural institutions. Museum legitimacy depends on sustained perceptions that institutional conduct meets professional, custodial, and public-mission expectations [5–7]. These perceptions were historically shaped through professional evaluation, editorially mediated news coverage, and direct encounters between institutions and visiting publics. Platformization changes these conditions. Platform distribution systems help shape which controversies and interpretations become visible, while conflict-oriented content may receive greater circulation than routine institutional communication [1,49]. Comment infrastructures allow evaluations to accumulate asynchronously and remain accessible after the precipitating event. Cross-platform circulation also places the same controversy within different expressive conventions and community contexts. Observed differences in platform discourse may reflect a combination of content form, interaction structure, community convention, distribution systems, and visibility or moderation practices. The analysis does not identify the independent causal effect of any single platform mechanism. Museum legitimacy is consequently contested within communicative conditions that remain only partly addressed in institutional theory and museum studies.

Distributed accountability is used here in a function-based sense to analyze the public-side organization of accountability pressure in platformized institutional crises. Prior scholarship has used the term in the context of multilevel governance to describe accountability distributed across multiple actors and governance arrangements [50]. The present framework shifts the analytical object from the distribution of accountability relationships to the distribution of substantive public demands for institutional response. Accountability research defines accountability through relationships in which actors must explain and justify their conduct before evaluating forums [31,32]. Crisis communication research shows how responsibility attribution shapes anger, reputational threat, and expectations for organizational response [12–14]. Platformization adds communicative environments in which data infrastructures, algorithmic curation, interfaces, and community conventions influence the visibility and circulation of evaluative expression [20,21,43]. Distributed accountability refers to the concurrent production of functionally differentiated demands for institutional responsiveness across these environments.

Platform environments may influence the relative visibility and prevalence of these functions through content distribution, interface affordances, content formats, and community conventions [1,9,10]. The functions remain analytically independent of any particular platform. Each function can appear in any platform corpus, and one corpus may contain a mixed profile across several functions. The framework does not assume that one function must predominate in every environment. Distributed accountability therefore describes the functional disaggregation of public judgment under platformized communication. It identifies concurrent demands generated around one institutional crisis and permits comparison of their relative salience across communicative environments. Platform environments are treated as mediating conditions, not as constitutive sources of particular accountability functions. Accordingly, differences in observed function distributions are interpreted as contingent associations within platform-specific corpora, not as evidence that platform architecture determines the form of accountability expressed by users.

The source files contained 88,552 comment observations. After comment-level deduplication, exclusion of empty-text and post-cutoff records, and removal of nested replies, the locked modeling corpus contained 64,349 top-level comments, including 28,146 from Douyin, 17,319 from Bilibili, and 18,884 from Rednote. Across event nodes, 25,442 comments were assigned to Node A, 24,784 to Node B, and 14,123 to Node C. The initial clustering solution contained 149 substantive topics and one outlier label. A total of 23,593 comments (36.66%) were initially classified as outliers. Probability-based reassignment assigned 1,370 of these comments to substantive topics, leaving 22,223 final outliers (34.54%). After topic reduction, the final BERTopic solution contained 49 substantive topics and one outlier cluster. The 49 substantive topics comprised 42,126 comments and formed the basis of the topic-level analyses. The targeted sensitivity analysis showed high agreement among documents classified as non-outliers in both the baseline and alternative specifications (common-nonoutlier ARI = .934 to .951). Agreement across all documents ranged from ARI = .564 to .879 and AMI = .787 to .949, while raw HDBSCAN outlier rates ranged from 33.63% to 37.17%. These results indicate that the clustering structure among consistently retained documents was comparatively stable. Outlier assignment was more sensitive to parameter variation. As specified in the Methods, the sensitivity analysis evaluates the UMAP–HDBSCAN clustering stage. It does not evaluate the final reduced 49-topic solution.

The six groupings can be interpreted through the three overlapping layers of public judgment proposed in the analytical framework. An affective reading is supported by topic-representation terms foregrounding ridicule, mockery, absurdity, and spectatorship, including Topics 13 and 30. Responsibility-oriented content is visible in topics organized around reporting, investigation, accountability, and personalized blame, including Topics 5, 7, and 12. Legitimacy-oriented content is reflected in topics organized around public distrust, perceived cover-up, and delayed justice, including Topics 0, 17, and 35. These examples illustrate how the three-layer framework can be used to interpret the topic solution. They do not constitute a separate classification of topics or comments into the three layers, and the study does not estimate the prevalence or overlap of these layers.

The cross-platform results also caution against assigning a distinctive emotional register to any single platform. The stable cross-platform finding concerns relative composition. The absolute ordering of accountability functions changed across coding specifications. Douyin showed a comparatively stronger punitive orientation, and Bilibili showed a comparatively stronger knowledge-based orientation across the specifications examined. These patterns are consistent with the possibility that content formats, comment interfaces, community conventions, and distribution systems condition which forms of evaluative expression become more visible, but they do not establish that platform architecture determines users’ affective responses. Content format and comment interfaces are directly observable characteristics of the three platforms, while community conventions and expressive habits provide plausible interpretations consistent with prior research [4,65]. Algorithmic distribution may also affect visibility, but recommendation processes were not observed directly in the present study. Algorithmic effects are therefore treated as a possible mechanism. They are not an empirically identified cause. Affective publicness is therefore best understood as a cross-platform layer of public judgment that becomes articulated through different combinations of moral evaluation, responsibility attribution, and institutional critique.

Punitive accountability helps explain how public dissatisfaction can become a structured pursuit of responsibility. Expressions calling for strict investigation, investigation teams, insider theft, and cross-jurisdictional inquiry appeared frequently across the corpus, with investigation and punitive accountability accounting for a larger share of substantive-topic comments in Nodes B and C than in Node A. At the platform level, punitive accountability was relatively over-represented in the Douyin corpus. Punitive accountability is treated here as the accountability function through which the attribution of responsibility becomes action-oriented. It translates blame into demands for investigation, sanction, and visible correction. As prior research has shown, the intensity of attribution shapes anger, loss of trust, and punitive expectations, while higher perceived responsibility increases demands for stronger organizational accountability [12,38].

The platform comparison likewise revealed relative differences without a one-to-one correspondence between platform and accountability function. Punitive accountability accounted for 36.84% of classified Douyin comments and was strongly over-represented relative to the pooled distribution. Its corresponding shares were lower on Bilibili (27.31%) and Rednote (29.89%), where punitive accountability was under-represented relative to expectation. Bilibili instead showed a relative concentration of knowledge-based accountability. Across the three corpora, responsibility claims kept questions of institutional answerability visible [9,41]. Punitive accountability mattered because it transformed diffuse dissatisfaction into more explicit demands for institutional answerability and corrective action. Expressions invoking insider theft, unresolved closure, or the necessity of strict investigation connected the discrete operational problem to broader judgments of managerial disorder and institutional failure [66]. Responsibility claims extended from specific individuals to museum management and broader cultural-heritage governance structures, consistent with research showing that high-intensity attribution can spill over into wider judgments about related organizations and institutional arrangements [67]. Interpreted through the responsibility-attribution lens, the topic structure suggests that public accountability can extend from particular actors to institutional procedures and governance capacity, while the measured visibility of punitive demands varies across communicative settings.

For cultural institutions, legitimacy concerns more than image. It depends on the capacity to sustain professional authority, public support, and social justification [5,8]. Once a crisis affects donation relationships, collection management, and internal governance, a case-specific controversy can escalate into broader judgments about institutional standing [7,29]. Cultural institutions are especially vulnerable because their standing depends heavily on the balance among professional authority, public mission, and institutional norms [15,30]. Topic content concerning trust, institutional credibility, perceived cover-up, and delayed justice provides an empirical basis for interpreting legitimacy questioning in the corpus, including evaluations of whether the museum remained a credible custodian of donated cultural property. Expressions of trust collapse and reluctance to donate extend the object of evaluation beyond short-term reputation to questions of custodial standing, institutional credibility, and the durability of public trust. Transparency, accountability, and sustained responsiveness are therefore central to legitimacy in contemporary cultural institutions [7].

Platform comments functioned as a mediating space between the attribution of responsibility and legitimacy pressure, carrying criticism beyond the immediate event and into broader evaluations of governance capacity, public standing, and institutional fitness. Legitimacy-oriented topic content appeared across all three event-anchored settings, indicating that institutional credibility was not confined to discussion surrounding the final official findings. This content appeared alongside themes concerning donation ethics, authenticity disputes, investigation demands, and personalized blame, providing a basis for interpreting legitimacy questioning as one dimension of the broader topic structure. For cultural policymakers and governance boards, this pattern suggests that legitimacy repair may require public explanation and investigation together with visible attention to collection governance, donor relations, and institutional transparency. Comparable museum crises suggest that legitimacy repair may require public explanation, independent review, and visible governance reform [68,69]. These examples are illustrative only and do not imply that comparable institutional responses would produce the same effects in the present case. The analysis does not establish whether particular institutional responses caused the observed legitimacy concerns, nor whether those concerns increased or declined over time. It shows only that legitimacy-oriented topic content was present across the three event-anchored source-content groups; the analysis does not establish its prevalence as a separately measured dimension.

This finding deepens existing understandings of platform public discourse. Platform publics are continuously organized through comment culture, content form, and community norms [4,49]. Platform environments provide different communicative conditions under which particular formulations of accountability may become more visible, repeatable, or salient [1,70]. Existing research provides several platform-specific mechanisms that can contextualize these differences. On Douyin, visibility is organized around engagement-sensitive recommendation and short-form production conventions that encourage creators to optimize immediate attention, retention, and algorithmic legibility [71]. This visibility environment offers one plausible context for the relative punitive concentration observed in the Douyin corpus. On Bilibili, video-centered participation has developed alongside distinctive community conventions, including time-synchronized danmu practices and ritualized forms of collective commentary that support interpretive and participatory community formation [53]. The present dataset contains top-level comments; danmu comments were not analyzed. Danmu practices form part of the wider communicative environment in which Bilibili users encounter and discuss public issues. Rednote combines user-generated content production with strong search and discovery practices and an explicit cultural emphasis on useful and authentic sharing, creating a communicative environment in which experiential accounts, practical information, and credibility judgments can become salient [72]. These mechanisms are literature-grounded interpretations of the platform environments and were not measured directly in the present study. The small platform–function effect sizes therefore support a contextual interpretation in which the observed distributions are compatible with differences in platform visibility and interaction conventions but do not identify the causal contribution of recommendation systems, community norms, or user composition. Platform moderation also conditions what can be observed. The corpus contains only comments that were publicly visible and retrievable at the time of collection. Comments removed, collapsed, or otherwise made unavailable before collection are not represented in the dataset. Cross-platform differences therefore describe retrievable public discourse and may reflect moderation and visibility practices as well as differences in user expression.

Each function operates independently of any particular platform as an analytical category. Each operates with its own evaluative criteria, affective register, and demand structure. Punitive accountability concerns sanctions and the enforcement of consequences. Knowledge-based accountability concerns procedural propriety and the integrity of institutional reasoning. Ethical accountability concerns moral commitments and the integrity of relational obligations. These distinctions have antecedents in pre-digital accountability scholarship [31,34]. What platformization adds is the concurrent production of these differentiated forms at scale across multiple communicative environments. Platform environments remain analytically relevant because the relative salience of these functions differs across platform-specific corpora. The present findings demonstrate patterned association without deterministic correspondence. The cross-platform differences concerned relative weighting within a shared three-function structure. The results do not support a one-to-one correspondence between platforms and accountability functions. Platform environments may therefore mediate or amplify the relative visibility of particular accountability demands without determining which functions are present or dominant. Such mediation may operate through content formats, distribution systems, interface structures, community conventions, and the composition of visible participation, although the present design does not identify the independent contribution of any one mechanism. Accordingly, the framework separates the substantive function of an accountability demand from the communicative environment in which that demand becomes visible. It therefore preserves the analytical independence of accountability functions while allowing platform environments to be examined as conditions associated with their relative distribution. This separation makes the framework empirically testable across different platform ecologies and institutional settings.

The broader relevance of the framework can be considered through institutional controversies in other national and organizational contexts. The 2023 disclosure of long-term theft from the British Museum provides a useful comparative reference because it likewise concerned custodial responsibility, collection management, and institutional trust. The controversy generated questions about leadership accountability, inventory and security procedures, and the museum’s wider claims to custodial authority. These dimensions correspond conceptually to the punitive, knowledge-based, and ethical demands distinguished in the present framework, with calls for consequences corresponding to punitive accountability, scrutiny of inventory, documentation, and security procedures to knowledge-based accountability, and debates over custodial legitimacy and restitution to ethical accountability. The comparison does not imply that the distribution of these functions across English-language platforms reproduces the pattern observed in the Nanjing Museum case. The comparison illustrates how the three-function framework may travel to another museum crisis in which institutional legitimacy rests heavily on custodial competence and public trust [68,73].

The Sackler donation controversy offers a complementary extension because the locus of accountability differs. The present case centers on the responsibilities of a museum toward donated cultural property and donor relations. The Sackler controversy concerned the ethical implications of museums accepting and publicly recognizing donations associated with contested sources of wealth [74]. Demands to remove donor names can be understood as punitive in the sense that they seek visible institutional consequences; scrutiny of due-diligence and donation-acceptance procedures raises knowledge-based questions about institutional decision making; and disputes over whether such funding is compatible with museums’ public missions raise ethical questions about legitimacy and moral obligation. The comparison suggests that distributed accountability may be useful for custodial controversies and for donor-related crises in which different forms of institutional responsibility become simultaneously salient.

The position carries several implications. Theoretically, it locates distributed accountability as a property of platformized public judgment, not of any specific platform ecology. The concept, therefore, offers a basis for comparative analysis across national contexts and institutional types whose legitimacy depends on sustained public trust. Methodologically, productive cross-context comparison should focus on identifying the conditions associated with the relative salience of particular accountability functions. Comparative studies across platforms such as TikTok, YouTube, and X could examine whether the coexistence of accountability functions observed here persists under different platform conditions and whether similarly modest or stronger platform-related differentiation emerges. For institutional practice, crisis response strategies should be both function-aware and platform-aware. Platform awareness should not be reduced to assigning a predetermined response type to each platform. An institution facing simultaneous punitive, knowledge-based, and ethical accountability pressures requires distinct response capacities for each, since each demands different forms of justification, evidentiary support, and communicative registers.

To meet punitive accountability pressure, institutions need established protocols for cooperation with regulators and inspection authorities, rapid disclosure of the status of investigations, and visible procedural steps early in a crisis response. Generic regret statements without procedural specificity may be insufficient when public demands center on investigation, responsibility, and visible corrective action. Knowledge-based accountability requires different capacities. Institutions need designated subject-matter spokespersons, publicly accessible provenance and collection management documentation, and transparent explanations of relevant procedures, including deaccessioning, transfer, appraisal, and disposal standards. Ethical accountability shifts the focus toward public mission and donor relationships. Museums need donor relationship protocols that specify notification requirements before disposal, transfer, or deaccessioning actions involving donated objects, along with structured pathways for apology, remediation, and engagement with donor families, descendant communities, or source communities. Ethical accountability accounted for a substantial share of classified comments in each platform corpus under the primary specification. Relational repair, custodial credibility, and the restoration of trust should therefore remain part of crisis response alongside factual clarification and procedural accountability.

At the governance level, museums and supervising authorities need institutional arrangements that can detect and respond to functional differentiation in real time. A cross-platform discourse monitoring function, reporting to senior leadership and governance boards, can identify changes in the relative prominence of punitive, knowledge-based, and ethical accountability demands. Such monitoring should compare the composition of accountability demands within and across platforms. Fixed communicative roles should not be assigned to particular platforms. The small platform–function association observed here indicates that platform differences are meaningful but limited, and that all three accountability functions may require attention within each platform environment. Annual transparency reports on collection management decisions can make procedural conduct verifiable before controversy emerges. Periodic external audits of custodial practices, donation processing, and historical record management can sustain governance credibility across leadership transitions. Crisis response playbooks should be organized by accountability function, with separate response capacities for sanction-oriented demands, evidence-oriented critique, and relationship-oriented repair. Platform-specific adaptation can then be applied at the level of format, timing, and presentation. The underlying response should remain aligned with the accountability function being expressed.

This study examined the Nanjing Museum donated-artifact controversy using 64,349 cross-platform top-level comments to analyze how public judgment forms in platformized institutional crises. The topic solution supports an interpretive reading in which affective expression, responsibility attribution, and legitimacy questioning appear together within the same thematic groupings. The measured findings concern the distribution of six thematic groupings and three accountability functions. All three accountability functions were present in each platform corpus, while their relative weighting differed across platforms. The absolute ranking of the functions was sensitive to the classification of Topic 0. The relative punitive concentration on Douyin and knowledge-based concentration on Bilibili remained stable across alternative coding specifications. These differences were statistically detectable and limited in magnitude. This pattern supports the interpretation of platforms as mediating conditions. It does not support treating particular platforms as determinants of specific accountability functions. Cultural institutions facing platform crises therefore confront multiple accountability demands with distinct response requirements.

The study makes three contributions. Theoretically, it brings together institutional crisis governance, accountability theory, and platformization theory to conceptualize distributed accountability as the functionally differentiated production of public accountability pressure in platformized institutional crises. Empirically, it shows how six thematic groupings are distributed across event-anchored discourse settings, and how punitive, knowledge-based, and ethical accountability are distributed unevenly across the Douyin, Bilibili, and Rednote corpora without forming one-to-one platform-function relationships. The principal empirical contribution therefore concerns the organization of accountability discourse across platform environments, not a universal ordering of the three accountability functions. Practically, it identifies institutional design measures for museums, supervisory authorities, and comparable trust-dependent organizations, including function-specific response capacities, donor relationship management protocols, cross-platform discourse monitoring, and governance review cycles attuned to punitive, knowledge-based, and ethical accountability pressures. Extending the framework requires cases in other platform ecologies and institutional fields, where the same three functions can be coded and their relative distributions compared.

passages.text: Large-scale, integrative databases are increasingly central to research on human evolution and deep prehistory [1]. Kintigh and colleagues [2] proclaimed, that the grand challenges in archaeology require systematically collected data, modeling and synthetic research. Addressing questions that span hundreds of millennia and entire continents requires data infrastructures that combine archaeological, paleoanthropological, paleoenvironmental, and chronological evidence within a unified spatio-temporal framework. The ROCEEH Out of Africa Database (ROAD [3]) was developed precisely to meet this challenge, providing a curated, relational repository of information on the deep human past across Africa and Eurasia between 3,000,000 and 20,000 years ago. This resource has been widely used, especially in recent years (see https://www.zotero.org/groups/5497463/roceeh/library). While ROAD offers a powerful web-based interface for data exploration and manual downloads, many contemporary research questions require programmatic, reproducible, and extensible workflows. Increasingly, archaeological inference relies on computational pipelines that integrate multiple data sources, apply transparent transformations, and enable replication and reuse [4,5]. In this context, the lack of a native scripting interface to ROAD has represented a significant bottleneck. The roadDB R package was developed to bridge this gap. It provides structured, script-based access to ROAD data directly within R [6], allowing researchers to integrate ROAD seamlessly into reproducible analytical workflows. In doing so, roadDB lowers barriers to accessing the ROAD database; it paves the way for multi-scalar and interdisciplinary research about the early human past based on transparent, reproducible analytical workflows.

These developments widened the scope of prehistoric research in terms of demography [10–13] and the evolution of material culture over hundreds of millennia and continental scales [14–17]. The growing reach of paleoenvironmental reconstruction allows the study of the early associations between cultural expression and environments [18–22], environmental resources [23] or the interaction of early humans with other taxa [24]. A variety of ecological niche models has been applied to estimate the potential distribution of diverse human species or cultures [25–43] and the niches of faunal taxa [44,45]. By combining paleoanthropological datasets, one can study the drivers of macroscale biological evolution of hominin species [46]. Geographical expansions are modeled by means of least cost path (LCP) and agent-based modeling (ABM) [47–50]. Increasingly, machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) permeate all fields related to the quantitative study of human prehistory [51].

Since the ROAD database is constantly evolving and the roadDB snapshot is updated regularly, we recommend saving a local copy of the queried tables. This ensures reproducibility, even if a later snapshot yields different results. Furthermore, we recommend validating the data retrieved from roadDB, for example by consulting the original literature (available through road_get_publications()) and searching for newer publications not yet included in ROAD. Note that ROAD is curated by experienced researchers and trained research assistants at ROCEEH, but may still contain errors. The information is recorded to closely follow the interpretations of the original literature and does not reflect the opinions of the curators. Nevertheless, some subjective choices had to be made, as the database is sourced from over 150 years of literature in diverse languages and research traditions, which naturally introduces a degree of ambiguity.

Open science has become a central concern across archaeology, particularly as research increasingly relies on large datasets and computational methods. Marwick and colleagues [5] argue that traditional archaeological publications often prioritize final results over the analytical processes that produced them and thereby leave key decisions about data selection, transformation and modeling implicit or undocumented. In computational research, this lack of transparency substantially limits reproducibility as even minor undocumented choices can strongly influence results. From this perspective, reproducibility is not a binary property but a spectrum ranging from studies that present only narrative interpretations and figures to those that provide data, code, and fully executable analytical workflows. Moving archaeological research along this spectrum requires not only open access to publications and data, but also open methods: scripted, inspectable, and reusable analytical procedures implemented in transparent software environments. Programmatic access to data plays a key role in this transition. While many archaeological datasets are now openly available, they are often accessed through manual downloads, interactive web interfaces, or undocumented filtering steps. Such workflows hinder reproducibility by making it difficult to reconstruct exactly which data were used and how they were selected. Here a shift from data ownership to data stewardship, in which researchers treat datasets as shared community resources and document their analytical use in ways that facilitate verification, reuse, and extension is called for [4,5].

The roadDB package directly supports this approach by embedding access to ROAD within a scripted R environment. Queries to ROAD become explicit, shareable code, rather than undocumented actions carried out through a graphical interface. This makes data selection and filtering part of the analytical record and allows workflows to be rerun, modified, and audited. By operating within R, an open-source environment widely used for reproducible research, roadDB aligns with best practices for transparent computational analysis. In addition, roadDB supports the FAIR data principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable). ROAD records are retrieved through structured queries, improving findability and accessibility. Outputs are returned as tidy data frames, enhancing interoperability with other analytical tools in the R ecosystem. Reusability is supported by clear documentation of function behavior, argument values, and database versions, enabling researchers to specify precisely which data release underpins a given analysis. By lowering the barrier between a complex relational database and reproducible analytical workflows, roadDB provides another way of using ROAD as an active component of open archaeological science. In doing so it provides a concrete implementation of the open methods agenda, demonstrating how curated macroarchaeological databases can be integrated into transparent, repeatable, and extensible research pipelines.

passages.text: Citizen Science (CS) is the public participation in the gathering of scientific knowledge [1,2]. On one hand, it should be viewed as a way to foster scientific education and public commitment to science, but it is also about people, without formal professional training, collecting scientific relevant data [3]. Our focus on this study is on the quality of biodiversity data that can be gathered by CS. The type and amount of information generated with CS can vary within areas of science, such as in ecology, geology and astronomy. One of the reasons for the recent spread of CS is the advance of technology, both hardware (cameras and powerful cellphones) and software (Artificial Intelligence to allow species recognition). Both price reduction and ease of use of these technologies have allowed CS individual and community initiatives, empowering a larger public to produce scientific information. It is reasonable to expect that CS will reach beyond the limits of traditional science, allowing data to be produced by a much larger public. Furthermore, scientists not trained in a given field can participate in data collection in other areas and therefore CS can also be considered as a transdisciplinary initiative [4].

One promising area where CS can contribute is in the assessment of biodiversity. The use of photography and CS can accelerate biodiversity studies [5]. Biodiversity reduction and habitat loss are some of the main problems of the world at the moment. One of the most affected environments in the world is the Atlantic Forest in Brazil. The Atlantic Forest (“Mata Atlântica”) is a tropical biome that spans most of the Brazilian coast. In southeast Brazil it occurs in the mountain regions, with a high level of rain and high number of endemic species. Remarkably, in Brazil, only ~15% of the original Atlantic Forest area remains [6]. Furthermore, there is an extensive reduction in the number of species, and several species are threatened with extinction [7]. This disturbing scenario drove us to study the biodiversity of this endangered biome with a hands-on approach, taking advantage of combined recent technological innovations. We decided to evaluate, in a CS perspective, the diversity of species of a privately owned property, an Atlantic Forest area in the mountains of Petropolis, near the city of Rio de Janeiro (Brazil).

There are several ways to assess the biological species in a given area: photographs, physical traps, visual observation, and sound records. Among these techniques, photographs have the advantage of being completely harmless and non-invasive to animals. The modern photographic capabilities allow for night images, using infrared light, and long-distance images, based on stabilized telephoto lenses. Moreover, photographs are now digital and with high resolution. The change from negative to digital imaging revolutionized photography, particularly in terms of cost and quality. Nowadays, the cost of obtaining and storing digital images is very low, and the use of images has pervaded our culture. Animal registration began very early (circa 1884) after the invention of photography, but to catch images of wild animals in nature has always been a challenge [8,9]. This burden has been lessened by digital photography and the reduction in cost of high-quality telephoto lenses, which are nowadays of very high light sensibility and digitally stabilized. Common cellphones now have powerful high-resolution cameras and large memory storage capabilities. In particular, camera traps with autonomous register capability were developed, and nowadays have very short response times (in the range of 0.5 seconds), infrared nocturnal detection and imaging and low cost.

Among the various species identification applications, we choose iNaturalist, Merlin and Addax. The iNaturalist (iNat) platform is a successful example of the power that CS can have in the acceleration of biodiversity research [10]. iNat is a nonprofit social network of naturalists and citizen scientists built on the concept of mapping and sharing observations of biodiversity, developed by the National Geographic Society together with the California Academy of Sciences. The importance of gathering biodiversity information around the world is enormous during the global warming and extreme climate changes that our planet has been undergoing in the last decades [11]. Biodiversity data, such as those generated through CS initiatives, are playing an increasingly important role in providing the necessary data for biodiversity assessments [12,13]. iNat is contributing to the increase in the collection of biodiversity data everywhere by common citizens [14]. Merlin is an automated bird-sound classifier that runs on mobile devices. It has been developed by the Cornell Lab of Ornithology. Merlin identifies birds in a region by combining the specific GPS location and date with the vast eBird database of bird observations, using this data to filter possibilities by size, color, and time of year for its powerful Sound ID (using machine learning for sounds). We also used the software Addax AI to classify the assembly of our data [15]. Addax has been used to process camera trap data in several protected areas worldwide. Interestingly, both Merlin and Addax use directly the raw images registered by the hardware, while iNat uses images processed by the user (images are usually cropped and their brightness and contrast corrected). All the applications are free or on a voluntary contribution basis.

We collected data from Plantae, Animalia and Fungi, in a 6 year-survey on the biodiversity of the Brazilian Atlantic Forest. We analyzed amphibians, arachnids, birds, insects, mammals, mollusks, reptiles and crustaceans. Due to their intrinsic characteristics, we used complementary approaches to observe and acquire information about organisms from distinct groups. Plants were photographed mostly with cellphones; birds were registered with professional cameras with tele-objective lenses and with the cellphone app Merlin (https://merlin.allaboutbirds.org/). Mammals were mainly registered with automated camera traps, either during day or night. Small animals (insects, arachnids and crustacea) and fungi were photographed with professional cameras with macro lenses or with cellphones. All specimens were afterwards deposited and classified in the iNaturalist application (https://www.inaturalist.org/) or classified in the Merlin application. Images from camera traps were also analyzed with Addax software.

One weakness of our study was the absence of observations of bats (Chiroptera). Since we used only non-invasive methods (photographs, videos and sound recording) to observe animals, we were not able to photograph bats. Bats are very hard to photograph because they are usually nocturnal and fly very fast. Collecting bats and other mammals in nature traditionally employs specialized equipment like fine-mesh mist nets, which can unfortunately inflict distress on animals [28]. Although we did not collect any Chiroptera, we were able to see bats several times flying in the area of study at sunset. Cronemberger and colleagues [29] described the presence of twenty-three species of Chiroptera in the Serra dos Órgãos National Park (Teresópolis and Petrópolis, RJ, Brazil), a nearby preserved and large Atlantic forest biome. Another group of mammals that is under-represented in our study are rodents, which are considered difficult to observe and classify due to their high diversity and small morphological differences [30]. Although we recorded rodents with camera traps, we could not classify them on the basis solely of the image, and we did not include them.
