passages.text: Global climate change, exacerbated by human activities, has resulted in the ongoing degradation of both the structure and function of terrestrial ecosystems [1,2]. As a fundamental component of these ecosystems, vegetation plays a crucial role in influencing regional ecological security through its functions such as carbon sequestration, soil and water conservation, and biodiversity maintenance [3–6]. The current warming climate and the increasing frequency of extreme events have accelerated processes like deforestation and vegetation degradation. Mountain ecosystems, characterized by their vertical gradients, are particularly vulnerable to climate change; phenomena such as shifts in forest belts and changes in species composition have emerged as significant ecological warning signals. In this context, accurately analyzing the spatiotemporal evolution and vertical differentiation patterns of vegetation cover is essential for informing effective ecological management strategies.

Fanjing Mountain is recognized as the “ecological gene bank at 27°N latitude” [7–9]. However, in recent years, climate warming and drying, along with increased human disturbances, have resulted in blurred boundaries between forest types and disordered vertical belt spectrum within this region. Traditional monitoring methods are constrained by limitations in temporal and spatial resolution as well as the complexity of the terrain, making precise and dynamic assessments challenging. Conventional vegetation surveys depend on ground plots and manual interpretation; while these approaches yield high data accuracy, they are hindered by elevated costs, lengthy timeframes, and inadequate large-scale continuity [10]. Remote sensing technology has enabled extensive monitoring of vegetation coverage through spectral indices such as NDVI [11–15], yet the presence of clouds in mountainous environments leads to significant data loss in optical remote sensing. Furthermore, existing algorithms demonstrate insufficient adaptability to complex terrains [16]. Although multi-source data fusion techniques can partially mitigate the limitations associated with single datasets, challenges regarding spatio-temporal consistency and model robustness persist. The Google Earth Engine (GEE) platform offers a new paradigm for long-term ecological monitoring due to its PB-level remote sensing data capabilities and cloud computing advantages [17–19]. however, its potential application for optimizing mountain vegetation classification models and analyzing vertical belt spectrum remains largely unexplored. Additionally, understanding the coupling mechanisms between changes in vegetation coverage and carbon cycling alongside climate feedbacks—along with elucidating the regulatory role of forest vertical belt spectrum in energy balance—continues to be at the forefront of research endeavors [20,21]. Current studies still exhibit deficiencies related to multi-source data fusion processes, terrain correction methodologies, and quantification efforts concerning vertical belt spectrum within mountain ecosystems.

From 1987 to 2007, the average Fractional Vegetation Cover (FVC) remained approximately at 55%, exhibiting a continuous downward trend with a cumulative decline of 12.35%. Following 2007, the average FVC increased to 64% as early macroscopic ecological engineering (such as the Grain for Green program) began to mitigate vegetation degradation. However, the region. However, the region experienced significant fluctuations from 2008 to 2013, reaching a low of 52.38%, reflecting the vulnerability of the early recovering ecosystem to natural climate disturbances, notably the severe ice and snow disaster in 2008. Since 2014, it has entered an ecological restoration phase, with FVC showing a notable increase to 66.65%, coinciding with and directly driven by strict conservation policies initiated during the World Heritage application in 2013. It peaked historically at 73.76% in 2016, characterized by dominant high coverage levels. Although there was a slight decrease to 66.08% in 2022, this figure remains significantly higher than early levels, indicating that the year 2007 marked a critical turning point resulting from the interplay of natural and human factors, and that an evident trend of ecological recovery has been observable since 2013.

From 2007 to 2022, a notable trend of improvement was observed, with the area exhibiting enhancement increasing to 442.98 km2 (57.15%). This improvement transitioned from being concentrated in specific locations to becoming more widespread across the entire region. The area demonstrating extremely significant improvement reached 57.45 km2, primarily distributed in the central and southern sections of the heritage site as well as in the northeastern part of the buffer zone. Conversely, areas showing insignificant improvement constituted the largest proportion at 31.29%, indicating a gradient pattern of enhancement extending from the heritage site into the buffer zone.The extent of degradation decreased to 135.79 km2, reflecting a reduction of 60.63% compared to previous periods. The remaining degraded areas have become increasingly marginalized and fragmented over time. Overall regional stability has improved, with basic stability encompassing an area of 196.36 km2 (25.33%), predominantly situated within the high-altitude core region.

passages.text: At first glance, the above-cited examples may create the impression that any relationship between social complexity and assemblage diversity is distinct and heavily context-dependent [22]. Therefore, a formal description of such distinct relationships would require different models. However, we argue here that the observable variability in the empirical evidence results from the same underlying dynamic behavior and may be described by a single mathematical algorithm. The presented model scales social complexity to production and consumption, and investigates the synergetic impact of cultural transmission and production biases on variations in material culture sets. However, our analysis of the impact of threshold parameters on the model behavior leads us to caution in clearly distinguishing social dynamics signals from other factors determining curve progressions in archaeological data.

Cultural traits are inscribed into objects made by people, for people [59,60]. Therefore, this study breaks down social complexity into a producer-consumer relationship and considers that producers are most frequently also the consumers of their own products, especially in small-scale societies. Unlike a cultural trait forced into a certain taxonomic unit (see below), an individual may participate in several groups of consumers and producers simultaneously. The latter is somewhat captured by the categorization of craft organization, e.g., part-time vs. full-time [41,42]. Here, we limit our model to stylistic variation, assuming only quantitative changes in consumer-producer relationships. For the sake of simplicity, the model considers only a single category of the produced and consumed objects, leaving the aggregation of the overall production and consumption as the combined signal of social complexity for future research.

Material culture assemblages are the aggregates of sub-assemblages, sub-sub-assemblages, etc., combining spatially and chronologically bounded sets such as artifacts, features, and sites [20]. Originating from information theory and widely applied in various fields of science, diversity measures are the aggregates of variation in assemblages. This aggregation is often quantitatively approached through the estimation of gamma diversity borrowed from ecology. Gamma diversity integrates alpha diversity, which is the diversity of individual assemblages, and beta diversity, representing a magnitude of sample variation [10,20,61–65]. This study avoids the issue of estimating beta diversity by introducing a simplification into the model: samples are considered homogeneous. In other words, we set beta diversity to 1, gamma diversity equals alpha diversity, and we describe our hypothetical assemblage as being composed of identical sub-assemblages.

While being quite intensively explored in archaeology [39–43,100–107], standardization as a production bias is often overlooked by models of culture change that may lead to a possible misinterpretation of the observed trends [81]. At the broadest scale, standardization – occurring as an increase in uniformity with increasing replication rates – is associated with a change in the organization of production coming with economic specialization and, therefore, consumer-producer ratios (e.g., [41] and references therein). Scaling to the individual unit of production (e.g., individual craftsman or workshop), the increase in replication rates results in a decreasing amount of time invested in a trait’s production. This ‘time-saving’ leads to a fall in the variation of traits produced by an individual unit below the inter-unit variability, which is confirmed by the empirical evidence [105–107]. However, we should underline that the association of standardization and increasing social complexity requires a certain caution. Intentional factors causing standardization may result from a general increase in the production scale but may not be associated with a change in the consumer-producer ratio [100,102].

A trajectory from the variability in pottery ornamentation towards monochrome black painting through the decrease in the combination of incising and painting, and the number of colors demonstrates ‘time-saving’. Also, this trajectory is indicative of the decrease in the use of wood as fuel for vessel firing. The frequency of the most time-consuming combination of incisions and polychrome painting decreases between c. 4100 and 4000 BCE, while the proportion of incised decoration (not combined with painting) increases between c. 4000 and 3950 BCE [112,113]. These changes indicate the decrease in use of calcium-based white paint in combination with mineral-based black and red paint, necessitating the firing of vessels twice at different temperatures [117]. The shift towards monochrome painting in the entire WTC corresponds to increasing settlement size [108,109,118–120], which fits the expectations of our model regarding standardization as an outcome of increasing production. It should be noted that the WTC example also demonstrates different factors simultaneously affecting the diversity at different levels of taxonomic hierarchy. Therefore, conditional diversities in ‘complex traits’ and their impact on the joint diversity at different scales [16,121,122], from an individual object to sets of objects, is a prominent topic for future research.

passages.text: Rice (Oryza sativa L.) is the principle staple cereal food for more than half of the population of the world with largest cultivation, production and consumption are contributing by South and Southeast Asia like (China, India, Bangladesh, Vietnam, Thailand, Pakistan, Malaysia etc). Cultivation of rice in these region, is typically characterized by diverse agro-ecological conditions, multiple cropping seasons and strong dependence on monsoon driven climatic variability [1]. These climatic heterogeneity profoundly influences the growth of rice, dynamics of pest population as well as the activity of natural enemies. The stability and productivity of rice is crucial for ensuring food security, compliance sustainable global economic and social development. But the cultivation of rice mostly depends on biotic and abiotic constraint, variety, management practice and climatic variables.

In addition, rice agroecosystem occupies a diverse abundance of rice arthropod species, with insect pests and natural enemies. Among biotic constraints, the abundance of insect pests in rice fields remain a major threat to sustainable rice production and responsible for substantial yield losses. Sap feeding insects likes planthoppers and leafhoppers, internal feeders like stem borer and gall midge, foliage feeders includes leaf folder and caseworms and grain feeders like rice bug are particularly destructive under favorable environment conditions [2–5]. The dynamics of these insects population are highly sensitive to weather variables like temperature, rainfall and relative humidity, which are directly responsible for mating, reproduction, survival and dispersal [3,6,7]. Consequently, fluctuation of temperature often result in seasonal pest outbreaks, particularly during monsoon period and rice transitional phases.

The interaction between insect pests and natural enemies with weather variables are intricate and often species specific. Temporal variables can accelerate pest reproduction and development while simultaneously enhancing or constraining predator activity, whereas relative humidity and rainfall may favor foliage feeders but negatively impact predator foraging efficiency or survival [12]. Despite growing acknowledge these interaction, majority of current research focuses on individual pest species of single seasons, offering little insight into the integrated dynamics of insect pests and natural enemy population across multiple cropping seasons and climatic variables. But, insect population behavior and trophic interactions in rice ecosystems are further modify due to altered rainfall patterns, increasing temperature variability and shifting monsoon dynamics in the context of climate change [3,6,13]. Therefore, proper understanding the abundance of insect pests and natural enemies according to weather variable and seasons is therefore critical for development and forecasting of climate-resilient and ecologically based integrated pest management strategies.

The pattern of observed monthly and seasonal weather variables are consistent with the tropical monsoon climate governing rice based agroecosystems in Bangladesh and similar South Asian regions. Higher maximum, minimum and mean temperatures from March to October, with peaked during from April to July, coincide with the pre-monsoon and monsoon periods. Moreover, the lower temperatures from November to February reflect the irrigated winter season. January is the coldest month in Bangladesh. After winter periods the temperature became increased from March-April and the gap between maximum and minimum temperature observed narrowed, which increase the activity of insect pests due to concludes the hibernation and migration of insect pest towards grasses and rice fields for the initial reproduction phase [3]. The concentration of rainfall and high relative humidity between May to October, especially during June and August, fit to the southwest monsoon period. Therefore, during these months the high humidity and frequent rainfall create favorable microclimatic conditions for herbivorous insect pests and simultaneously influence the activity, survival and dispersal of natural enemies [3,8,15]. Seasonal comparisons of weather variables further revealed that the Aus season experienced with the highest temperature and rainfall, followed by Aman and Boro seasons, which reflects distinct agro climatic situations which influence insect abundance across rice growing seasons. Moreover, Boro season also experienced with very cold temperature and increased high temperature also. Such seasonal thermal periods are well documented and play a critical role in regulating the phenology of rice as well as the population dynamics of insects [3,6].

Understanding the ecological interactions of rice insect pests and their natural enemies under changing climatic conditions is essential for the development of effective, ecologically based pest surveillance and management techniques. The six year longitudinal study, spanning from January 2019 to December 2024 offers crucial insights into the seasonal and monthly fluctuations of major insect pests and their natural enemies concerning major climatic factors. The Shannon-Wiener diversity index (H´) serve as a reliable measure for assessing the biodiversity of insect pests in a group. The H´ value of 2.16 signifies a modest diversity of rice insect pests and natural enemies, whereas maximum potential diversity (H max = 2.89) and evenness index (E = 0.75). The brown plant hopper (Pi = 0.3469) exhibited significance prevalence among insect pests, representing the largest proportion to overall community diversity. This supremacy highlights that BPH is presently the principal ecological catalyst of pest pressure in study area of Bangladesh, especially in intensive rice farming, elevated nitrogen fertilizer application and conducive climatic conditions that enhance BPH proliferation while compromising ecosystem stability [3,16,17]. The green leafhopper (Pi = 0.1267), white-backed planthopper (Pi = 0.1084) and yellow stem borer (Pi = 0.0679) were the subsequent most prevalent pests. Among the natural enemies, the staphylinid beetle (Pi = 0.0766) was the most abundant, and green mirid bug (Pi = 0.0614) and carabid beetle (Pi = 0.330) were the subsequent natural enemies.

Furthermore, natural enemy populations also exhibited strong temporal and seasonal pattern. The abundance of natural enemy closely related with the abundance of harmful species. Predators like carabid beetles and ladybird beetles peaked mainly in October-November, coinciding with the peaked abundance of prey insects during the Aman season. This temporal composition suggests density dependent responses of predators to prey availability a key composing mechanism in rice agroecosystems [20,21]. The maximum abundance of staphylinid beetles exhibited during December-March month (winter season) which is under the Boro season, indicating their preference for lower temperatures which further confirmed by their negative association with temperature variables. Moreover, odonates (dragonflies and damselflies) were most abundant during the Aus and the Aman seasons, coinciding with high humidity, rainfall and the availability of aquatic habitats made by monsoon rainfall, which are essential for their development of larva [3,22,23]. Spider, non-significant monthly and seasonal variation, maintained relatively stable populations throughout the year, which indicating their normal predatory behavior and resilience across varying climatic conditions. Spider an ecological indicator, which reflects environmental health and biodiversity due to ability to thrive across seasons underscores their role in pest management and balance of the ecosystem [3,12,24].

Weather variables poses both direct and indirect effects on insect pests as well as natural enemies abundance. Temperature positively associated with dragonflies and field cricket abundance, highlighting temperature dependent development and flight activity of odonates [22]. Moreover, temporal variable were non-significantly but positively associated with most of the insect pests and natural enemies, except staphylinid beetle, green mirid bug and spider. In contrast, the significantly negative correlation of staphylinid beetles with temporal variables suggesting their vulnerability of thermal stress. However, rainfall exhibited predominantly non-significant association with insect pests and natural enemies but tended to favor foliage-feeding insects like rice leaf folder and caseworm, likely through enhanced host plant growth and succulent leaves. Furthermore, rainfall negatively correlated numerous predator, due to disturbance physically, reduced efficiency of foraging or mortality of larvae [25]. On the other-hand, relative humidity a key climatic driver, positively influencing the abundance of damselfly while negatively affecting BPH, ZzLH, YSB and RB and predators like CBB, StPB and GMB.

Our findings showed significant positive interrelationships among most insect pests, highlight shared responses to favorable environmental conditions as well as crop phenology rather than direct boosting [3,11]. In contrast, natural enemies exhibited selective associations with specific insects likes; spiders were positively correlated with leaf folder, caseworm, yellow stem borer, rice bug and long-horned cricket highlight the vast key role of spiders for inhibition of pest populations. Carabid beetle and green mirid bugs were showed positive association with planthoppers and leafhopper, which consistent with their role as key predator of sap-feeding insects and mostly prey egg, larva and adults of these insects [8,25]. Damselflies exhibited positive correlation with rice leaf folders, caseworm and long horned cricket; while dragonflies exhibited positive association, rice bug, stem borer, planthoppers and leafhoppers. Conversely, natural enemy showed negative correlations also with insect pests. These intricate correlation among natural enemies with multiple pest species indicate their broad predatory range.

Despite present study provides a comprehensive assessment of insect pests and natural enemy dynamics for six years by using light trap, but it was performed at a single monitoring site utilizing a solitary light trap. Moreover, dependence on light trap data could lead to an underrepresentation of non-phototactic or day active species and may not accurately reflect true field numbers. Consequently, the observed abundance trends and climatic associations mostly represent the ecological circumstances of the study location and should not be generalized to all rice cultivation areas. In addition, insect populations are affected by local agro-ecological factors such as planting time, cropping intensity, rice cultivars, adjacent flora, landscape diversity, management techniques and regional climate fluctuations. Moreover, agricultural performance metrics like grain production, yield reduction, and economic thresholds were not explicitly assessed in conjunction with insect populations, complicating the quantification of the exact productivity effects of certain pest infestations. Although the extensive temporal dataset enhances assurance in the seasonal patterns observed at this site, the quantitative estimates of insect population may differ under different environmental circumstances. Future research should incorporate direct field sampling techniques, assessment of yields and economic injury threshold analysis to enhance pest prediction models.

Light trap is an effective instrument for monitoring of insect population in a particular crop field. Particularly, nocturnal insects including planthopper, leafhoppers, rice leaf folder, caseworm, stem borer are capture by light trap, and can also use as a pest management tools in IPM strategy when the activity of insect pests are peaked [26]. In IPM strategy, the proper monitoring of insect pest populations plays a crucial role and light trap is one of the appropriate monitoring tools [27,28]. We used light trap to track the monthly and seasonal abundance of rice insect peat and natural enemies. Light trap captures mainly nocturnal species, that’s the main drawback of light trap. Moreover, the efficacy of light trap influence by night length, trap design, size, height, kind of bulbs use and weather variables including temperature, humidity, rainfall during trapping, wind, cloud cover and moonlight. The synchronization between pests and natural enemies highlights the potential of ecologically based IPM strategies which leverage climatic forecasting and enhance sustainable rice production under changing climate scenario.

This six year light trap monitoring study at Bangladesh Rice Research Institute (BRRI), Gazipur demonstrated that seasonal dynamics of insect pests and natural enemies under the local rice agro-ecosystems. The peak activity period of insect pests found in two times in a year; a) April-May and b) September-November and coinciding with the reproductive stage of Boro and Aman season, respectively. Among the seasons, Aman season found as most abundance season of insect pests. The observed temporal patterns also showed clear associations with seasonal weather conditions, suggesting that climatic variability and crop phenology jointly influence insect activity at BRRI Gazipur monitoring site. So, the identification of peak period time including months and seasons particularly the Aman season and the transitional periods, provides critical windows for proper monitoring and intervention of insects. So, by integrating proper monitoring, conservation of natural enemy, long-term climatic scenario and IPM strategy may reduce pest populations naturally. Future studies integrating light trap monitoring with field infestation assessments, economic threshold analyses and evaluations of biological control and IPM interventions will be essential to determine whether these seasonal patterns can be translated into practical pest management recommendations.

passages.text: Pollination, and more specifically insect pollinators, are essential to healthy ecosystems and play a critical role in both crop production and the reproduction of many flowering plant species. Nearly 70% of leading crop species experience increased production when pollinators are present [1]. The European honeybee (Apis mellifera) often receives the most attention and recognition as a pollinator. However, A. mellifera is only one of over 20,000 species of bee documented worldwide [2]. In contrast, other species, such as bumble bees, mining bees, mason bees, and leafcutter bees, are under-studied and under-appreciated despite evidence that native pollinators such as these are more effective than honey bees at pollinating a number of flowering crop species [3–5]. Native solitary bees such as Osmia lignaria have even been developed as managed crop pollinators in North America [6,7]. These bees also exhibit a diverse array of life histories, ecological niches, and nesting habits. The majority (roughly 90%) of bee species are solitary [8] and build nests in soil (ground nesters) or dead wood, stems, or piles of brush (cavity nesters) [9]. While some native bees are generalists, gathering resources from a wide array of flowering plant species, some are specialists, and will only collect pollen from a select few species [9]. This intricate dependence on specific plant species and habitat structures makes native pollinators vulnerable to habitat loss and human disturbance [9].

One increasingly popular tool to help mitigate these problems for native pollinators is the pollinator hotel. While the majority of solitary bee species are ground nesters (approximately 70%), pollinator hotels can serve as habitat for the remaining 30% of cavity nesting species [10]. These structures are also commonly called bee hotels, but they often host a variety of solitary wasps as well as cavity-nesting bees [11]. Mason bees (Osmia spp.) and leafcutter bees (Megachile spp.) are the two most common genera reported utilizing pollinator hotels [11]. Mason wasps (Vespidae: Eumeninae), grass carrying wasps (Isodontia spp.), and square-headed wasps (Crabronidae) are also frequently observed inhabiting the hotels [9]. While bee species provide valuable pollination services, solitary wasps found in pollinator hotels also contribute to controlling pest insect populations [12].

Pollinator hotels replicate cavity nesting species’ natural nesting sites by offering access to hollow tubes, often made of bamboo, reeds, cardboard, drilled wooden blocks, or the stems of native plants [9]. Providing the bees with a diverse array of materials may help to attract a wider range of bee species [14]. However, each material type has its own unique attractants and drawbacks. Drilled blocks, for example, are known to be extremely attractive to both bee and wasp species but are difficult to maintain [15]. Any old nests left in the blocks may contain diseases or parasites that are impossible to completely remove. Likewise, positioning the drilled holes too near to the edges of the block can make the nests susceptible to parasitism, especially by the Leucospis affinis wasp [16]. Bamboo or reed tubes with too large a diameter may be either left completely unoccupied or preferentially host large non-native bees such as the aggressive giant resin bee (Megachile sculpturalis) [14]. Cardboard tubes are commonly available in commercial nest kits, but very high rates of parasitism have been reported [17].

Regular maintenance is also essential. Many pollinator hotel maintenance practices have extensive anecdotal evidence, but are not backed by empirical data. For example, emergence boxes are small, mostly enclosed containers in which nest materials can be placed to provide a transitional area where the bees can emerge [9]. The old nesting materials can then be removed and cleaned over the winter while the bees are inactive. In the summer, the bees emerge and are free to make nests in fresh materials in the main hotel. These boxes often come with commercial pollinator hotel kits, but there is little to no empirical evidence that demonstrates whether the boxes are an effective tool for pollinator hotel maintenance. There are risks that creating an even greater concentration of nest sites within the emergence boxes can encourage parasitism, or that the emerging insects will return to nest in the boxes rather than the newly-cleaned hotels. This lack of data matters because cleaning pollinator hotels is an essential maintenance task. Chalkbrood and parasitic mites can linger in old nests and spread throughout the pollinator hotel without regular cleaning [17]. Other parasites, such as Houdini flies, beetle larvae, and parasitoid wasps may also accumulate in pollinator hotels without regular maintenance [17].

Parasitic and parasitoid wasps are a common secondary inhabitant of pollinator hotels [9,17,22,23]. The most common of these are Monodontomerus species (Torymidae), L. affinis (Leucospidae), and members of the family Chrysididae. Monodontomerus wasps are tiny parasitoids that lay their eggs in Osmia and Megachile nests [17]. Leucospis affinis also parasitizes the larvae of Osmia and Megachile, along with some species of solitary wasps [22]. Members of the Chrysididae family are common kleptoparasites of several pollinator hotel residents [24,25]. There is some indication that parasitism may be more common in pollinator hotels than in dispersed nesting sites, and that this increase may correlate with the higher density of nest sites that pollinator hotels encourage [13,26,27]. Parasitism in pollinator hotels can disproportionately affect the native bee residents of the hotel, rather than introduced bees or either native or introduced wasp species [13]. If left completely unmanaged, pollinator hotels may become more of a liability to their native, solitary inhabitants [13]. To be effective tools, pollinator hotels must be installed and maintained on a regular schedule, using tools to both preserve the native bee populations and reduce the burden of parasites and parasitoids.

In this study, we investigated the parasite burden present in four pollinator hotels. We also conducted the first empirical study on whether emergence boxes could be implemented as an effective maintenance and cleaning tool. We first conducted a biodiversity study of a single pollinator hotel in North Carolina to understand inhabitant profiles. Secondly, we surveyed the parasite burden across four pollinator hotels. We hypothesized that the parasite burden would be highest in cardboard nest tubes as previously described, but that nests made of reeds would also have a higher parasite load than bamboo tubes because of the relative thinness of the reed tube walls. Lastly, we tested the efficacy of emergence boxes as a maintenance tool. Specifically, we evaluated whether nests placed in emergence boxes would accumulate futher parasitism and whether bees and wasps would construct new nests inside the old materials in the boxes. In half of the emergence boxes, we implemented a one-way valve that we hypothesized would further reduce the rate of bees re-entering the emergence boxes.

The results of the biodiversity survey (Study 1) show that the UNC Asheville pollinator hotel is home to a wide variety of bee and wasp species, but that diversity is unevenly distributed across the hotel. The numbers of observed insects were distributed unevenly throughout the twelve sub-boxes in the hotel as indicated by a chi-square test of independence, but there were no trends across rows or columns of sub-boxes. Additionally, there were no significant differences in the number of families across different areas of the hotel. This was an unexpected result because the upper row of the hotel (sub-boxes 1-4) are shaded by the roof for several hours after the bottom rows have begun to receive sun. Orienting pollinator hotels towards the southeast is standard practice in North America and Europe, and nests with exposure to the morning sun are thought to be more attractive to bees [16], but in our study, the differences in sun exposure appeared to have little affect on overall trends in insect or family abundance.

These results also indicate that parasites are indeed very common in the pollinator hotel. Several of the material types surveyed in Study 1, including paper tubes and bamboo, had nearly the same number of parasitoid insects as non-parasitoid insects found inside. Previous research has found that paper tubes are particularly vulnerable to parasitoids, especially the parasitic wasp Monodontomerus obscurus [17]. Beyond parasitic wasps, birds and rodents have also been observed dismantling bee nests housed in paper tubes, consuming the larvae, and using the paper itself for their own nests [17]. Bamboo and reeds have previously been considered safer for bees, and the thicker walls of these materials can offer some protection from other common parasites like Leucospis affinis [16]. However, the high presence of parasitoids in these materials in the biodiversity survey indicates an underlying problem. Before the start of this research in 2022, the UNC Asheville pollinator hotel had not been properly maintained or cleaned since its construction in 2016. Regular maintenance is necessary to prevent the buildup of parasites and diseases in pollinator hotels [9], and the absence of this maintenance likely explains the large number of parasites observed. These results, while striking, likely overestimate the number of parasitoid insects present in the pollinator hotel, as only adult insects were included in the data set. Unparasitized cocoons containing healthy larvae were therefore likely present but not counted. Nevertheless, the high prevalence of parasites was corroborated in Study 2, where insects were reared from nests rather than relying on a snapshot of adult presence.

The four families of parasites represented in Study 2 differed from those documented in the first study. Ichnumonid and Eulophid wasps were not documented in the first study at all (likely due to small size in the case of the Eulophids), while significant levels of L. affinis wasps and chrysidid were observed that were not then documented in the second study. Leucospid and chrysidid wasps were observed again in the emergence box study (Study 3), though in low numbers (one individual each). The discrepancies in the identified families between the three studies could be due in part to the sampling method. It could also be due to the confluence of factors contributing to nesting success – flight range, proximity and co-occurrence of resources, and other factors. The second study used only nests made in new, undamaged nest materials that had only been in the pollinator hotel for two months. It is possible that leucospids and chrysidids are more prone to parasitizing damaged materials, or that the positioning of the new tubes in tight bundles made it more difficult for the wasps to penetrate them. Leucospid wasps, specifically, rely on ovipositors to penetrate up to 3/4 of an inch into the outside of a nest to reach the bee’s cocoon [16]. The materials located towards the inside of our material bundles would likely have been inaccessible to the wasps, which may have influenced the types of parasites seen in the study.

The patterns of parasite burden observed across the eulophid and torymid species were more expected. The far higher abundance of parasites observed in paper tubes as compared to bamboo and reeds fits both with our hypotheses and with previous research that paper tubes are more susceptible to parasitism [17]. Eulophid wasps were also more common in bamboo nests than reed ones. However, as there was no significant difference between the levels of Torymid wasps present in reeds versus bamboo, we are unable to fully support our original hypothesis that reeds are more susceptible to parasitism than bamboo. The susceptibility of bamboo to parasitoids in general is much less well studied than the susceptibility of paper tubes. Further, we are prevented from making determinations about the reasons behind the greater burden of eulophid wasps in bamboo tubes by the obscure nature of the wasp itself. The species of wasp observed at the pollinator hotel was identified as belonging to the family Eulophidae, genus Melittobia, by the Plant Disease and Insect Clinic (NC State University). However, the species was unable to be determined, and the life history and host(s) of this wasp are unknown. Future research should also include the effects of diameter as a covariate factor that may affect overall parasite abundance in addition to material type.

The patterns of parasite burden across the four pollinator hotel locations were less expected. Torymid and eulophid parasites displayed nearly opposite trends. The levels of eulophid parasites were orders of magnitude lower in the three NC State hotels than the UNC Asheville hotel. Torymid wasps (specifically Monodontomerus obscurus) which occurred in significantly greater numbers in all three NC State pollinator hotels, are known parasitoids of Osmia and Megachile bees [17]. Parasitoid wasps have been suggested to be especially susceptible to host competition because of their reliance on limited hosts to complete their reproductive cycles [47]. While both M. obscurus and many wasps in the eulophid genus Melittobia are generalists, and thus able to parasitize a variety of host species [48–50], the limited number of hosts within the pollinator hotel may still lead to interspecific competition. Additionally, since the hosts are more concentrated in the pollinator hotel than they would usually be in the wild, the wasps may have reduced barriers to finding hosts [47]. Many species of wasps have been shown to co-parasitize the same larva, even if only one species can ultimately develop [51]. If the torymid and eulophid wasps were engaging in co-parasitism or subjected to increased interspecific competition due to the increased population density of the pollinator hotel environment, competitive exclusion of torymids by the eulophids may have occured at the UNC Asheville hotel.

One of the primary concerns with emergence boxes as a tool to reduce parasite burden was the risk of confining healthy, unparasitized nest cells in the same small space as parasitized cocoons. Because parasitoids such as Monodontomerus have shorter generation times than their hosts, they can multiply greatly over a single season in a bee hotel or emergence box. If the parasitoids were able to hatch before most of the bees, the box itself might serve as an accelerator of parasitism, since it increases population density even more than in the hotels itself. The increased population density of pollinator hotels has been previously linked to increased risk of parasitism [26]. However, small numbers of new parasitoid holes were observed across all three treatments at the end of the emergence box study, which indicates that parasitoid wasps did not eclose and parasitize bee cocoons before the bees themselves were able to leave the boxes. While some nest tubes did increase parasitoid holes over the study, the data were heavily skewed towards zero levels, indicating that additional parasitism inside the emergence boxes was uncommon. This bodes well for the success of emergence boxes as a maintenance tool.

The other main concern with emergence boxes is the potential for bees to re-nest inside them. While an emergence box is in use, the rest of the materials in the hotel can be cleaned and replaced as needed to reduce the buildup of parasitoid wasps, mites, and fungal pathogens [9]. Cavity-nesting bees seek protected cavities to nest in, and, if the bee has just emerged from an emergence box, it may decide to return to the box to make its new nest. In the third study, while the proportion of bees that re-nested in the emergence box was not zero, it was low (at or below 12.5% when mud type changes are included, at or below 4.6% when mud type changes are not included) across all three treatments. This indicates that the great majority of bees that hatch out of the emergence boxes found another area (presumably the cleaned and refreshed pollinator hotel nearby) to make their nests in. Most of these re-nesting events consisted of transitions between different types of mud caps, rather than transitions from resin, leaf pulp, or grass. This indicates that mason bees, rather than leafcutter bees, resin bees, or grass wasps, likely return to nest in the emergence boxes most frequently. However, because the mud color changes could potentially be due to environmental effects and because every type of material underwent at least one re-nesting event, no definitive conclusions can be drawn about which families of bees are most likely to re-nest in an emergence box. Additionally, because insects were identified only to the family level and because of the relatively small number of nest materials that were reared out in the lab, we were unable to make concrete connections between particular groups of bees and their relative likelihood to re-nest in the emergence boxes. Insects were unable to be further identified to genera and/or species due to the damage samples sustained while in storage from sustained power outages associated with Hurricane Helene.

Taken together, the results of these three studies highlight both the ecological complexity and management challenges of artificial nesting habitats for solitary bees. Patterns of biodiversity and parasitism at the UNC Asheville pollinator hotel reveal how environmental orientation, maintenance history, and material choice shape community composition and parasite load. The differences in parasitoid prevalence and family across the four hotel locations underscore the strong influence of site-specific factors and potential interactions among parasitoid species. Finally, the emergence box experiment demonstrates that these tools may allow for pollinator hotel maintenance without significantly increasing parasitism risk or encouraging extensive re-nesting within the emergence boxes themselves. While certain behaviors, such as limited re-nesting, merit further study, the overall findings suggest that careful placement, regular cleaning, and the strategic use of emergence boxes can enhance the long-term health and sustainability of managed pollinator populations.

Our results should be used to improve the maintenance practices for pollinator hotels because of their value not only as conservation tools, but as educational platforms that can shape public understanding of native bee ecology. Pollinator hotels are ideal venues for students, citizen scientists, and the broader community to directly observe species interactions and the consequences of different management decisions. Effective pollinator hotel management contributes to sustaining native bee populations that are integral to the reproduction of both wild and managed flowering plants systems. As habitat loss and anthropogenic pressures continue to threaten pollinator communities globally, initiatives that integrate research, maintenance, and public education can help foster ecological literacy while directly supporting pollinator preservation. In this way, well-managed pollinator hotels can function not only as nesting habitat but as living classrooms that connect local conservation actions to global concerns about biodiversity, ecosystem resilience, and our agricultural system.

passages.text: The levels of phenotypic variability observed in this study are consistent with those reported in pearl millet diversity panels evaluated across West Africa and the broader semi-arid tropics [12,30], confirming that the Senegalese germplasm captures a representative range of genetic diversity for the traits studied. The high CV for grain yield reflects the phenotypic heterogeneity of the panel entries rather than residual segregation; this heterogeneity is expected given that the panel draws on entries from different breeding sources. The relatively low variation in flowering time compared to yield-related traits follows a pattern widely documented in pearl millet, where photoperiod sensitivity and adaptation to terminal drought impose strong directional selection on phenology while leaving morphological and yield traits more open to diversification [31].

Heritability estimates across traits were consistent with the quantitative genetic architecture expected for pearl millet under Sahelian conditions. The relatively high H2 for grain yield indicates a substantial genetic basis for yield variation in this panel, comparable to values reported from combining ability and multi-environment studies in West African pearl millet [32], though the residual environmental component underscores the importance of multi-environment evaluation for reliable selection gains. The high heritability observed for panicle length and plant height reflects their predominantly additive genetic architecture and lower sensitivity to G × E interaction, consistent with findings across recombinant inbred line populations and diversity panels in pearl millet [33,34]. The moderate to high heritability for flowering time aligns with reports from Senegalese landraces [35], where photoperiod sensitivity introduces trial-to-trial variation while maintaining a meaningful genetic signal. These estimates suggest that direct phenotypic selection will be most efficient for morphological traits, while grain yield improvement will require multi-environment testing and genomic-assisted approaches to effectively capture and exploit the available genetic variation.

The phenotypic distribution across the GWAS panel revealed substantial variation for all four traits, consistent with quantitative inheritance and phenotypic ranges reported in pearl millet panels evaluated across West Africa and the semi-arid tropics [12,30]. The correlation structure reflected biologically meaningful associations consistent with patterns widely documented in pearl millet: the positive relationships among plant height, panicle length, and grain yield suggest shared developmental pathways and pleiotropic genetic control, while the negative correlation between flowering time and grain yield reflects the drought escape mechanism whereby early flowering confers yield stability under terminal drought, a priority selection criterion in Sahelian breeding programs [31]. These patterns support the use of indirect selection through morphological traits under favorable conditions and confirm early flowering as a key target for adaptation to the Senegalese rainfall pattern.

The genetic-diversity indices and the population-structure analysis were computed on complementary subsets rather than on a single panel, and are best read together. Gene diversity, PIC, observed heterozygosity, and inbreeding coefficients were estimated on the full genotyped set (279 genotypes), which still included early-generation segregating material, whereas the PAM/PCA structure analysis was restricted to the 137 advanced, genetically stable entries that formed the association panel. The moderate gene diversity (GD) and PIC observed in both groups are consistent with previous SNP-based characterizations of pearl millet germplasm, where these indices typically range from 0.20 to 0.40 depending on origin, breeding history, and marker density [12,36]. The slightly lower diversity in Group 1 (PMiGAP inbreds) relative to Group 2 reflects the cumulative effect of directional selection within the ICRISAT breeding program, since elite pools under sustained improvement predictably harbour narrower allelic ranges than locally adapted or multi-cross material [37]. Group 2, by contrast, is compositionally heterogeneous: check cultivars alongside multi-cross lines spanning early to advanced generations, and this breadth sustains higher allelic diversity through the accumulated recombination and residual segregation characteristic of early-generation material, accounting for its elevated GD and PIC. These contrasts bear directly on how heterozygosity was interpreted and how the association panel was assembled. The near-identical observed heterozygosity across the two groups is consistent with the allogamous, protogynous reproductive biology of pearl millet, and the moderate inbreeding coefficients confirm that the genotyped diversity set had not reached fixation. Because non-fixed genotypes violate the fixed-line assumption underlying single-marker association testing and can inflate association noise, the early-generation segregating material was excluded and the GWAS was restricted to the 137 stable entries; residual relatedness within that panel was then controlled through a kinship matrix in the mixed-model framework [38,39]. Finally, although the PIC values fall at the lower end of the moderately informative range [40], they remain adequate for association analysis given the large number of markers retained after quality filtering, while the minor-allele-frequency spectrum spans rare variants of potential relevance to adaptation in the Sahelian environment.

Population structure within the 137-entry association panel was weak and largely continuous. PAM clustering identified k = 2 as the silhouette optimum, yet average silhouette widths remained below 0.05 across all values of k, indicating that the panel does not resolve into sharply differentiated subpopulations. This near-continuous stratification is consistent with the panel’s composition, in which PMiGAP lines and local multi-cross material derived from ICRISAT parents share substantial ancestry rather than forming discrete pools. Soft genetic boundaries of this kind are expected in an obligate outcrosser, where protogynous flowering and wind pollination sustain continuous gene flow that prevents sharp discontinuities [41,42]. The low variance captured by individual principal components is likewise a known property of high-dimensional differentiation in outcrossing cereals rather than a shortcoming of the panel, and has been reported for comparable West African germplasm [36,37]

Methodologically, continuous stratification of this form favours fitting several leading PCs as fixed covariates together with a kinship matrix as a random effect, rather than a single Q-matrix, to control false positives while preserving detection power [43]. The panel therefore sits at a productive point in the diversity–stratification trade-off: its allelic range is broad enough to power association detection, while its structure is correctable rather than confounding. Association signals recovered consistently across the panel are expected to be the most transferable across the ISRA–ICRISAT breeding continuum. Finally, the faster LD decay characteristic of West African pearl millet relative to South Asian material [12,36] means associations from Indian panels do not transfer directly to this context, reinforcing the value of a regionally anchored reference panel for future multi-trait and multi-environment GWAS in the Sahelian production system.

Linkage disequilibrium decayed rapidly, with mean r2 falling below 0.1 at approximately 8 kb across the 14,718 SNPs scored in the GWAS panel, consistent with the outcrossing biology of pearl millet, in which recurrent recombination erodes marker–marker correlations over short distances. The reference PMiGAP diversity panel reported even faster decay (r2 < 0.2 within 84–444 bp), a rate comparable to allogamous maize [11]. The greater LD extent observed here is expected from the panel’s composition: unlike a largely panmictic diversity set, our panel combined advanced inbred lines with locally derived breeding material, several entries sharing pedigree and subject to directional selection, both of which reduce effective recombination and extend haplotype blocks. Such subpopulation-dependent variation is documented in pearl millet, where the West-African subgroup shows greater decay owing to a longer recombination history [36]. The short-range LD confirms that dense, genome-wide marker coverage is required to capture causal variants [44].

Eleven MTAs were detected across six chromosomes for the traits under study, each association individually explaining a modest fraction of the overall phenotypic variance. This distribution is characteristic of the polygenic, small-effect architecture typical of quantitative agronomic traits in pearl millet, and it aligns with prior genome-wide work in the crop: the reference GWAS across test-cross progenies identified 1,054 significant MTAs for fifteen traits, with individual associations explaining between 9% and 27% of phenotypic variation [11]. The only exception in our study was on chromosome 4, where the marker SNPPM6939 associated with grain yield explained 48.67% of the phenotypic variance and had a negative effect on yield. An effect of this magnitude is atypical for a quantitative trait and should be interpreted with caution: in a panel of only 137 entries with no independent validation population, single-locus effect sizes are prone to substantial overestimation (the Beavis effect), and the value may partly reflect minor-allele frequency or allele-class imbalance rather than a true major effect. This need for independent confirmation is reinforced by the deleterious-variant burden documented in Senegalese pearl millet [45], which argues for building association resources on regionally adapted germplasm and validating candidate signals before they are deployed in selection.

Several of other associations correspond, at the chromosome level, to genomic regions previously implicated in the same traits. Earlier marker-based studies in pearl millet associated marker alleles with plant height on linkage group 7, and with panicle length on linkage groups 2, 5, and 7, while a further allele on linkage group 7 was associated with grain yield [44], and more recent association analyses have likewise recovered agronomic-trait associations for plant height, panicle length, and grain weight in the crop [46]. This convergence of independent panels and marker systems on broadly overlapping regions is consistent with these being genuine effects rather than artefacts; the correspondence is, however, at the chromosome level and does not by itself establish that the same underlying loci are involved.

A notable feature of the present results is that chromosome 4 harbored associations for three traits: grain yield (SNPPM6939, 3.9 Mb), plant height (SNPPM8294, 128.2 Mb), and panicle length (SNPPM8661, 227.9 Mb), making it, together with chromosome 2, the most trait-rich region in the panel. This co-occurrence does not, however, imply a shared genetic basis. The three markers are dispersed across more than 220 Mb of the chromosome, with the plant-height and panicle-length signals alone separated by roughly 100 Mb. Because linkage disequilibrium in this panel decayed to r2 < 0.1 within approximately 8 kb, associations this far apart cannot be in linkage with one another and instead represent physically independent loci that merely reside on the same chromosome. The co-localization of plant height and panicle-related traits reported previously in pearl millet [47] therefore does not extend to the present associations, which show no evidence of a single pleiotropic region governing multiple traits. The functional candidates underlying each of these independent signals are considered below. Inspection of the ± 8 kb intervals flanking the significant markers nominated several functionally credible candidates, which should be regarded as hypotheses for subsequent validation rather than confirmed causal genes. Because these candidates were identified solely by physical proximity to significant markers within LD-defined windows, their positions localize but do not establish a causal relationship, and the links proposed below are positional hypotheses to be tested functionally. Two gene families recurred in the intervals flanking the plant-architecture and panicle associations: F-box domain proteins and AP2/ERF transcription factors. The AP2/ERF family is a well-characterized regulator of inflorescence development and yield in cereals: in rice, these transcription factors participate in the regulation of panicle architecture, grain plumpness, and yield formation by controlling inflorescence meristem activity, cell division, and differentiation [48], and their agronomic relevance extends across grasses, in wheat, mutation of an AP2/ERF gene (DUO-B1) regulating spike architecture increased grain number per spike and raised field yield without penalizing other major agronomic traits [49]. The presence of an AP2/ERF candidate near the chromosome 4 region jointly associated with plant height and panicle length would therefore be consistent with a role in meristem determinacy and inflorescence patterning, though this remains to be demonstrated. The F-box candidates are similarly noteworthy: in rice, mutations in the F-box gene LARGER PANICLE improve panicle architecture and enhance grain yield [50], and non-synonymous variants in both an AP2/ERF gene and an F-box domain-containing protein were recently reported to jointly explain a large proportion of the variance for panicle exsertion [51]. The recurrence of these two families in our intervals parallels that functional pairing and supports their prioritization as candidates for follow-up, rather than confirming their involvement in the panicle-related associations.

For flowering time, the strongest a priori candidate in pearl millet is the phytochrome pathway. Natural variation at PHYTOCHROME C is a long-recognized determinant of phenology and morphology in the crop: association studies first linked natural variation at PHYC to flowering time and morphological variation across a set of inbred lines [41], a result subsequently refined through fine-scale association mapping and analysis of linkage disequilibrium and selection in the vicinity of the PHYTOCHROME C gene [52]. This locus has since been repeatedly implicated in Sahelian adaptation, having been identified as a major flowering-time gene underpinning selection for earlier flowering in response to climatic variation [31]; it is cited here as regional context, as the flowering association recovered in the present panel does not fall within the PHYC region. Flowering time is highly quantitative [53], so the single association recovered here most likely reflects the limited power of a panel of this size under a stringent multi-locus threshold, rather than a truly simple genetic basis, with a larger panel expected to resolve more loci. It is nonetheless tempting to speculate that crosstalk between photoreceptor and auxin-mediated pathways contributes to the phenological variation observed here, a hypothesis consistent with documented phytochrome–auxin interactions in other species [54] but one that would require direct functional testing to validate.

This study reported a genome-wide association analysis of grain yield, plant height, panicle length, and flowering time in a Senegalese pearl millet panel combining internationally derived inbred lines with locally adapted breeding material. Eleven MTAs were detected across six chromosomes, several linked to genes plausibly involved in cell expansion, inflorescence development, and hormone-mediated growth. Because associations from South Asian panels transfer poorly to West African germplasm, these results are of particular regional value, with the plant height and panicle length loci and the large-effect grain-yield locus on chromosome 4 emerging as the most robust and promising targets for marker-assisted and genomic selection. Realizing that potential will depend on functional validation of the candidate genes and confirmation of the associations in larger, stabilized panels spanning a wider range of West African environments. This case is reinforced by the burden of deleterious variants carried in Senegalese pearl millet germplasm, which argues both for confirming candidate signals on this genetic background and for using maturing genomic resources to track and progressively purge these alleles from the breeding pool while preserving its regional adaptation. Carried forward into multi-environment testing, genomic-selection pipelines, and regionally important constraints such as downy mildew and Striga, these findings offer a grounded basis for genomics-assisted pearl millet improvement in Senegal and the broader Sahel.

passages.text: In high-producing dairy cows, microbial composition can vary throughout the estrous cycle, in response to natural hormonal changes that affect pH, vaginal secretion profile, and local immunity. These physiological oscillations can modulate bacterial composition and diversity, resulting in specific microbial profiles for each phase of the cycle [2]. However, the use of hormonal protocols for estrus synchronization, a practice widely adopted in intensive production systems, can significantly interfere with this natural dynamic [3]. Interventions with progesterone, estrogens, prostaglandins, and gonadotropins alter the vaginal environment by modifying mucus, blood flow, and the immune response, potentially producing artificial changes in microbial composition. These alterations can mask or attenuate spontaneous variations in the microbiota, making it difficult to understand its natural behavior and its real influence on fertility [4,5].

In addition, the literature indicates that certain bacterial communities can serve as biomarkers of gestation in cattle, thereby complementing the interpretation of our results. More stable microbial profiles with lower abundance of opportunistic pathogens have been associated with higher conception rates, while subtle changes in groups such as Ureaplasma and some fermenting families (e.g., Ruminococcaceae) have been linked to better conditions for artificial insemination, especially when related to favorable hormone levels during estrus [7]. Taken together, these studies reinforce the idea that the presence of specific taxa during gestation or at critical moments of fertility may reflect physiological adjustments specific to reproduction, corroborating the notion that microbial biomarkers, although subtle, carry functional relevance and can distinguish physiological phases with greater precision than isolated diversity metrics [9,28].

Finally, the absence of marked differences between phases and the clear predominance of individual effects underscore the importance of investigating the determinants of the “ideal” or functional microbial composition of the reproductive tract. Longitudinal studies that track microbial changes before, during, and after conception, as well as integrated approaches combining metagenomics, metabolomics, and physiological parameters, can substantially deepen understanding of the microbiota-fertility interaction. The presence of several genera (e.g., Fibrobacter) that are not consistently reported in this niche was unexpected, and further studies are necessary to determine whether it is of fecal origin. This knowledge will be important not only to advance the reproductive management of high-producing dairy cows, but might also have implications for the intestinal colonization of calves.
